risks.description: The log content, retention period, integrity protection and audience are not specified, so it is unclear whether it supports traceability of AI-influenced caregiver actions (for example, actions taken on AI-generated alerts) or is only a user-facing transparency feature.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: Specify the log schema (actor, role, action, timestamp, linked AI alert or recommendation ID), tamper-evident storage, retention aligned with Art. 19 and NFR-13.5, and who can view the log. Link entries to the AI outputs that triggered the caregiver action.

addressed_by.covers: audit logs for access to sensitive information, which partly captures caregiver access events
logging of AI-generated advice, which is the AI-output side of traceability

recommendations: Define the FR-8.6 log content, retention, integrity protection and viewer access, and cross-reference the AI-output logs in NFR-3.6 and the access logs in NFR-5.5 so caregiver actions can be traced to the AI outputs that prompted them.

requirement_text: The app shall use a simple and intuitive interface suitable for older adults.

assessment.summary: NFR-1.1 is a general usability statement for older adults. It is not an AI Act obligation in itself, and the SRS already covers accessibility, plain language, AI labelling and AI explanations elsewhere (NFR-1.3, NFR-1.7, NFR-2.x, FR-11.5, NFR-15.x). The only remaining point is that 'simple and intuitive' is untestable and is not linked to the Article 13 and 14 transparency and oversight obligations.

risks.description: 'Simple and intuitive' has no acceptance criteria, so there is no evidence that older adults can understand the AI outputs (urgency classification, recommendations) or use the override and challenge functions as Article 13 and 14 require.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately.
risks.engineering_action: Add measurable usability criteria, for example usability tests with older-adult participants. The tests should confirm users can interpret AI urgency outputs and use the dismiss and challenge controls. Keep the results as documentation evidence.

addressed_by.covers: explanation of why alerts or recommendations were generated
user ability to challenge, correct or dismiss AI suggestions
plain-language explanation of AI suggestions

recommendations: Replace 'simple and intuitive' with testable usability acceptance criteria. Include comprehension of AI outputs and ease of use of the override and challenge functions, and retain the test evidence.

requirement_text: The app shall support guided onboarding for first-time users.

assessment.summary: Guided onboarding is a useful vehicle for telling users what the AI features do and where they stop, but the requirement does not say what it must contain. Without that, users may start using AI health features without seeing the system's purpose, limitations or how to challenge outputs. The gap is one of wording and evidence, so it is low severity.

risks.description: Onboarding content is unspecified, so nothing ensures first-time users are told the AI features' intended purpose, limitations, accuracy and uncertainty, or how to override or challenge AI output.
risks.quote: The instructions for use shall contain at least the following information:
risks.engineering_action: Amend NFR-1.6 so onboarding covers: that an AI assistant is in use, its intended purpose and limits, not replacing professional care, uncertainty indicators, how to challenge or report AI output, and emergency use. Keep onboarding content versioned as evidence for the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: states that AI advice does not replace professional medical advice (intended purpose and limitations)
lets users challenge, correct or dismiss AI suggestions (the user-side override that the instructions should describe)

recommendations: Define the minimum onboarding content in NFR-1.6: AI disclosure, intended purpose and limitations, uncertainty indicators, how to challenge or report AI advice, and emergency guidance. Keep a versioned record of that content as transparency evidence.

requirement_text: The system shall support an increasing number of users without major performance degradation.

assessment.summary: NFR-10.1 is a generic scalability requirement with no measurable targets. The system is a health AI, so scaling can affect the accuracy and robustness of AI outputs, but other requirements already address AI scaling and responsiveness. The remaining gap is low severity and concerns wording only.

risks.description: The requirement sets no measurable load or performance thresholds and does not say that AI accuracy and robustness (e.g. urgency classification) must be maintained under growing user load, so "major performance degradation" cannot be verified or declared.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define quantitative load targets (concurrent users, latency percentiles) and add acceptance criteria that AI accuracy and urgency-classification quality are unchanged at target load. Include these in load and regression testing.

recommendations: Quantify NFR-10.1 with load targets and require that AI output accuracy and safety-critical functions (symptom urgency classification, emergency detection) stay within declared thresholds at those loads, verified by load testing.

requirement_text: The system shall support scaling of AI services during peak usage.

assessment.summary: The requirement covers scaling of AI services during peak usage, but gives no accuracy, robustness or fail-safe expectations under load. Scaling could degrade the safety-critical AI functions (symptom urgency classification, emergency detection) without anyone noticing.

risks.description: No requirement states that AI accuracy, urgency classification and emergency detection must be maintained under peak load, or how the system degrades safely when scaling limits are reached.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates.
risks.engineering_action: Add acceptance criteria that AI accuracy and the latency of urgency and emergency detection (FR-4.3, FR-7.5) are unchanged at peak load. Define a safe degradation mode, such as a rule-based fallback with a user notice, and load-test the AI components under peak conditions.

addressed_by.covers: graceful recovery from system errors (resilience to faults)
emergency information stays accessible during service disruption

recommendations: Extend NFR-10.2 with measurable criteria that AI accuracy and the latency of emergency and urgency functions hold under peak load, with a defined safe-degradation fallback, and verify them through load testing.

requirement_text: The app shall support integration with common wearable devices and health monitoring tools.

assessment.summary: encryption of sensitive data in transit and at rest

requirement_text: The app shall respect user autonomy and allow older adults to make their own decisions where possible.

assessment.summary: NFR-12.2 is a high-level autonomy principle with no testable behaviour, so it does not specify how the AI-driven features (symptom urgency classification, mood detection, caregiver alerts) leave the older adult in control. Other requirements cover challenge/dismiss and consent, but the autonomy statement itself is vague and not tied to human oversight design measures such as override and automation-bias safeguards.

risks.description: The requirement does not define concrete oversight measures (e.g. ability to disregard, override or stop AI outputs, awareness of automation bias) for vulnerable older users, and 'where possible' leaves the scope undefined and untestable.
risks.quote: to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Reword NFR-12.2 into testable criteria: the user can disregard, override or stop any AI recommendation or automated alert at any time, and the UI includes anti-over-reliance cues. Trace it to NFR-15.4, FR-10.5 and FR-8.3.

addressed_by.covers: ability to challenge, correct or dismiss AI-generated suggestions (14(4)(d) disregard/override)
user can request human assistance

risks.description: The autonomy requirement does not state how users are told the AI's capabilities and limitations, or how autonomy is preserved in automated caregiver alerts such as FR-8.3 and FR-2.4, which may not require user consent.
risks.quote: designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately
risks.engineering_action: Add acceptance criteria: users are informed of what the AI can and cannot do and which automated notifications go to caregivers, and consent or opt-out is explicit for each (extend FR-10.5 consent to FR-8.3 and FR-2.4).

addressed_by.covers: transparency about how AI decisions are made
explanation of why alerts or recommendations were generated

recommendations: Rewrite NFR-12.2 with measurable criteria for user override, opt-out and decision control over AI outputs, and add anti-automation-bias design measures.
Make caregiver notifications consent-based or opt-out for every automated alert and document the AI's capabilities and limitations for users.

requirement_text: The app shall clearly distinguish between AI advice and human clinical advice.

assessment.summary: The requirement states the AI/human distinction only in general terms. Most of the substance sits in NFR-15.3, FR-11.5 and NFR-3.1, so the remaining gap is a testable presentation standard and AI-interaction disclosure at the chat/voice level. Without it, older or cognitively impaired users could mistake AI output for clinical advice.

risks.description: Wording "clearly distinguish" has no measurable criteria, and it does not cover voice interactions or users with cognitive impairment. Users could still mistake AI outputs in the assistant for clinician advice.
risks.quote: providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite the requirement to mandate a persistent AI label on every AI message, text and voice (spoken disclosure), with distinct visual and audio styling and acceptance tests including users with reduced vision or cognition. Reference NFR-15.3 for source attribution.

addressed_by.covers: identifies whether advice came from AI, a caregiver, or a healthcare professional
indicates when recommendations are AI-generated
states AI advice does not replace professional medical advice

recommendations: Make NFR-12.3 testable: persistent AI labelling in text and voice, distinct styling, usability tested with older users, and cross-reference NFR-15.3 to avoid duplicate requirements.

requirement_text: The app shall be designed to support independence, not replace human care.

assessment.summary: NFR-12.5 is a high-level design principle with no verifiable criteria, so it does not by itself ensure that the app's AI functions (symptom urgency classification, mood detection, personalised recommendations) can be effectively overseen or overridden by humans. Most oversight controls already exist elsewhere in the SRS, so the remaining gap is mainly about making the principle testable and tied to those controls.

risks.description: The requirement states an intent (independence, not replacing human care) but defines no testable oversight measures, such as when AI outputs such as urgency classification or mood detection must be routed to a human, or how humans can intervene or stop the system.
risks.quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite NFR-12.5 with verifiable acceptance criteria (e.g. mandatory human escalation paths for emergency/urgent classifications, the user's ability to disregard AI outputs, and traceability to FR-14.5, NFR-8.6 and NFR-15.4), and add test cases.

addressed_by.covers: ability to challenge, correct or dismiss AI-generated suggestions (14(4)(d))
clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (14(4)(d))
user can request human assistance

recommendations: Make NFR-12.5 measurable by linking it to concrete oversight controls (human escalation for urgent and emergency classifications, override and dismissal, human assistance) and define how each will be verified.

requirement_text: The app shall maintain records needed for clinical safety audits.

assessment.summary: NFR-13.3 requires 'records needed for clinical safety audits' without defining which records, retention period, or integrity protections. Traceability of AI outputs and retention for a high-risk health system are therefore left undefined. NFR-3.6 and NFR-5.5 partly cover AI-advice and access logging.

risks.description: Record scope is undefined: it does not specify event logs (usage periods, inputs, model version, outputs, reviewer actions) that enable traceability of the AI classification and recommendation functions (e.g. urgency classification FR-4.3, emergency detection FR-7.5).
risks.quote: In order to ensure a level of traceability of the functioning of a high-risk AI system that is appropriate to the intended purpose of the system, logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for identifying situations that may result in the AI system presenting a risk
risks.engineering_action: Define a log schema covering AI inputs, outputs, urgency class, model/knowledge-base version, confidence, user challenge/dismissal, clinical reviewer actions and escalation events, and link it to NFR-3.6.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review (outputs only)

risks.description: No retention period is defined for audit records, and it conflicts with the data-deletion and minimisation requirements (NFR-13.5, NFR-4.1), so audit evidence may be deleted too early or kept too long.
risks.quote: Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent such logs are under their control.
risks.engineering_action: Specify a minimum retention period (at least six months, or longer under medical-device rules), pseudonymise logs, and reconcile with the deletion policy.

addressed_by.covers: general retention and deletion policy mechanism (no audit-log period defined)

risks.description: The requirement does not state that the technical documentation and records are kept up to date and available for the authorities, nor does it tie audit records to the post-market monitoring of safety incidents.
risks.quote: The provider shall, for a period ending 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service, keep at the disposal of the national competent authorities
risks.engineering_action: Add that audit records and technical documentation are retained for 10 years and can be produced on request, with tamper-evident storage.

addressed_by.covers: developer and administrator documentation (no retention or authority availability)

recommendations: Define the audit record schema covering AI inputs, outputs, versions and reviewer actions.
Specify retention periods for audit logs and reconcile them with deletion requirements.
Add 10-year retention and availability of documentation and records for authorities, with integrity protection.

requirement_text: The system shall maintain regular backups of user data.

assessment.summary: NFR-14.1 is a generic data-resilience control with no direct EU AI Act obligation; resilience, recovery and data-loss prevention are already covered by NFR-14.2, NFR-6.4 and NFR-5.1. Only minor wording clarifications could improve evidence for Article 15 resilience.

risks.description: Backup requirement does not specify scope (e.g. AI logs, model versions), frequency, integrity or restore testing, or whether backups are encrypted and access-controlled, which limits evidence of resilience and of retained AI logs.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates
risks.engineering_action: Define backup scope (including AI advice logs per NFR-3.6 and model versions), RPO/RTO, encryption and access control for backups, and periodic restore testing.

addressed_by.covers: disaster recovery procedures supporting resilience (15(4))
prevention of data loss during crashes or interruptions (15(4))
encryption of sensitive data at rest

recommendations: Clarify backup scope, frequency, integrity checks, encryption and restore testing, and include AI logs and model versions, to evidence Article 15 resilience.

requirement_text: The system shall support disaster recovery procedures.

assessment.summary: The disaster recovery requirement is generic. It sets no recovery objectives, restores no AI-specific components (models, logs, knowledge base), and defines no testing, so the system's resilience and the integrity of its safety audit trail are unverified after a major failure. The gap is moderate: backups (NFR-14.1) and emergency-info availability (NFR-14.5) exist.

risks.description: Disaster recovery has no measurable objectives (RTO/RPO), no scope covering AI model versions, the knowledge base, or safety guardrail configuration, and no testing, so the system cannot show it recovers to a correct, safe state for a high-risk health AI.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates.
risks.engineering_action: Define RTO/RPO per critical function, include model artefacts, knowledge base and guardrail config in the recovery scope, and require periodic DR drills with documented results.

addressed_by.covers: regular backups of user data (part of the technical redundancy solutions in 15(4))
emergency information stays accessible during service disruption

risks.description: Recovery procedures do not state that AI advice logs, audit logs and clinical safety records are restored with integrity, so the traceability record could be lost or corrupted after a disaster.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: Add to the DR scope that AI advice logs (NFR-3.6), access audit logs (NFR-5.5) and caregiver activity logs (FR-8.6) are backed up and restored with integrity verification and retention preserved.

addressed_by.covers: regular backups of user data, though it does not name logs

recommendations: Make NFR-14.2 measurable: set RTO/RPO, cover AI models, knowledge base and guardrails, and require tested DR drills.
State that AI advice, access and caregiver audit logs are included in backup and restore with integrity checks.

requirement_text: The system shall notify users of planned maintenance where possible.

assessment.summary: NFR-14.4 is an operational availability requirement about notifying users of planned maintenance. It has no AI Act compliance gap at requirement level, and related obligations (accuracy, robustness, transparency) are handled by other SRS requirements.

requirement_text: The app shall explain why important alerts or recommendations were generated.

assessment.summary: NFR-15.1 requires explanations for important alerts and recommendations but does not say who they are for, what they contain, or how accurate they must be. Health-related alerts and urgency classifications may be high-risk, and without these details explanations may be unusable for older adults, caregivers and clinicians, or unavailable for deployer oversight.

risks.description: The explanation is not specified in terms of content (main logic, inputs, limitations, confidence, accuracy) or audience (older adult, caregiver, clinician), so it may not let deployers interpret the output as Art. 13 requires.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately.
risks.engineering_action: Define explanation content per alert type (key input factors, urgency rationale, uncertainty, known limitations), tailor it to each role, and state the accuracy level and metrics of the underlying model in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: plain-language explanation of AI-generated suggestions to users
simple explanations of health trends
confidence or uncertainty indicators

risks.description: The requirement does not tie explanations to the specific inputs and model version that produced each alert, and no stored explanation record is required, so explanations cannot be reproduced for audit or incident analysis.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: Store the explanation, input features and model version with each alert or recommendation in the audit log, and make them retrievable for review.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review

risks.description: Explanations are not required to help overseers detect automation bias or to be presented so that users and caregivers can interpret and override urgent alerts, such as urgency classifications and emergency detection.
risks.quote: to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system’s output, taking into account, for example, the interpretation tools and methods available
risks.engineering_action: Show the explanation alongside each urgent alert, with an option to dismiss or challenge it, and test comprehension with older adult and caregiver users.

addressed_by.covers: users can challenge, correct or dismiss AI-generated suggestions
clinical review of high-risk AI outputs

recommendations: Specify explanation content, audience and accuracy or limitation disclosures for each alert type, building on FR-3.6, FR-13.3 and NFR-8.4.
Log the explanation, inputs and model version with every alert, extending NFR-3.6.
Show explanations next to urgent alerts with dismiss or challenge controls, and test comprehension with older adults and caregivers.

requirement_text: The app shall avoid creating false reassurance when symptoms may require medical attention.

assessment.summary: NFR-15.5 states a goal (avoid false reassurance) but sets no measurable criterion, test, or error-rate target for under-triage of symptoms. Without these, the symptom-urgency function cannot show it meets declared accuracy and robustness levels for a likely high-risk health AI system.

risks.description: No measurable accuracy or robustness metric (for example false-negative/under-triage rate for urgent and emergency symptoms) is defined or tested, so 'avoid false reassurance' cannot be verified.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite the requirement with a testable criterion, e.g. a maximum under-triage rate for urgent/emergency cases on a clinically validated test set. Add a conservative default that escalates when confidence is low, and re-test after each model update.

addressed_by.covers: escalation of potentially serious symptoms to emergency or professional care guidance
confidence or uncertainty indicators, relevant to avoiding overconfident output

risks.description: Accuracy levels and known limitations for symptom triage, including the risk of false reassurance, are not required to be declared to deployers and users in the instructions for use.
risks.quote: the level of accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity referred to in Article 15 against which the high-risk AI system has been tested and validated and which can be expected, and any known and foreseeable circumstances that may impact that expected level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
risks.engineering_action: Require the instructions for use and in-app information to state the tested triage accuracy metrics and the foreseeable circumstances that degrade them (incomplete symptom input, atypical presentations in older adults, comorbidities).

addressed_by.covers: statement that AI advice does not replace professional medical advice

risks.description: The risk of false reassurance is not tied to a risk management process that identifies, evaluates, and tests mitigations for foreseeable misuse and health risks, such as users delaying care after a 'low urgency' output.
risks.quote: the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose
risks.engineering_action: Add false reassurance to the hazard log with severity and likelihood ratings, linked mitigations, and acceptance criteria. Verify mitigations through scenario testing of low-urgency outputs for red-flag symptoms.

addressed_by.covers: avoidance of unsafe, overconfident or unsupported medical recommendations

recommendations: Define a measurable under-triage target and a validation test for urgent/emergency symptoms, with a conservative escalation default when confidence is low.
Declare triage accuracy metrics and known limitations to deployers and users.
Record false reassurance in the risk management file with mitigations and acceptance criteria.

requirement_text: The app shall comply with recognised accessibility guidelines such as WCAG 2.2 where applicable.

assessment.summary: NFR-2.1 sets a general WCAG 2.2 commitment. Accessibility by design for high-risk AI is required under Art. 16(l), and the requirement is supported by NFR-2.2 to 2.8 and FR-1.6. The wording is vague: 'such as' and 'where applicable' leave the conformance level and evidence undefined, which is a low-severity clarity gap.

risks.description: The requirement does not state a WCAG conformance level (A/AA/AAA), scope (including AI assistant voice and text interactions) or evidence of conformance, so compliance with the Art. 16(l) accessibility obligation cannot be verified or documented.
risks.quote: ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882
risks.engineering_action: Specify WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the minimum for all screens including the AI assistant, replace 'such as' and 'where applicable' with a defined scope, and record accessibility test results (automated and assistive technology testing) in the technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: screen reader support
high contrast display options
support for users with reduced vision, hearing, dexterity or cognitive ability

recommendations: Fix the conformance target at WCAG 2.2 AA, define its scope across all user-facing and AI interaction surfaces, and keep accessibility test evidence in the technical documentation.

requirement_text: The app shall allow users to slow down or repeat voice instructions.

assessment.summary: NFR-2.8 is an accessibility control that lets users slow down or repeat voice instructions. It is not an AI Act compliance gap, and it helps users understand and use the system's outputs.

requirement_text: The app shall escalate potentially serious symptoms to emergency or professional care guidance.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.2 requires escalation of serious symptoms but sets no accuracy target, no testing of the escalation logic (false negatives), and no definition of how a human can intervene. Missed escalations in a health-triage context for older adults could cause serious harm and block conformity assessment.

risks.description: No accuracy or robustness metrics, or acceptance thresholds (especially for false-negative escalation rate), are declared for the symptom-urgency detection that drives escalation.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define sensitivity/recall targets for emergency and urgent classes, test on representative older-adult data, and set release gates and regression tests for the escalation logic. Declare these metrics in the instructions for use.

risks.description: The escalation function is not tied to a risk management process that identifies and mitigates foreseeable harms such as missed or delayed escalation, over-escalation causing alarm, or misuse by vulnerable users.
risks.quote: The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Establish a documented risk management process covering escalation failure modes, with hazard analysis, residual-risk acceptance criteria, and lifecycle review. Link NFR-3.2 to it.

risks.description: The requirement does not state how users, caregivers, or clinicians can interpret, override, or question the escalation output. Related controls exist elsewhere, but escalation-specific oversight is not defined, such as handling of a suppressed or ignored escalation.
risks.quote: to be able to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system’s output
risks.engineering_action: Specify in NFR-3.2 that escalation messages include the reason and urgency level and that the user can dismiss them. Define how dismissals and missed escalations are logged and reviewed.

addressed_by.covers: explanation of why important alerts or recommendations were generated (14(4)(c))
ability to challenge, correct, or dismiss AI suggestions (14(4)(d))
clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (14(1))

recommendations: Set and verify sensitivity targets and acceptance criteria for escalation detection, particularly for emergency and urgent classes.
Create a lifecycle risk management process covering escalation failure modes and link NFR-3.2 to it.
Clarify in NFR-3.2 that escalation output shows its reason and urgency and can be dismissed, with dismissals logged for review.

requirement_text: The app shall include safeguards against hallucinated medical advice.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.4 asks for 'safeguards against hallucinated medical advice' but names no concrete mechanism, accuracy metric or test criterion, so it cannot be verified for a health assistant that likely counts as high-risk. Other requirements cover parts (grounding, logging, clinical review), but nothing sets measurable accuracy or robustness levels or tests for hallucination.

risks.description: The requirement does not define accuracy or hallucination metrics, acceptance thresholds or test methods, so the safeguard cannot be verified or declared in the instructions for use.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite NFR-3.4 to define a hallucination/factual-error rate metric with thresholds, an evaluation dataset covering medical queries, and pre-release and regression testing. Declare the results in the technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: grounding recommendations in reliable medical knowledge sources, which supports accuracy
avoiding presentation of uncertain outputs as facts

risks.description: No technical robustness measures are specified, such as grounding or retrieval checks, output validation against medication and clinical rules, or fallback to a safe response when confidence is low. Adversarial or erroneous inputs could also trigger unsafe outputs.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates
risks.engineering_action: Specify technical safeguards: retrieval grounding with source citation, rule-based validation of dosage and drug-interaction outputs, a confidence-based refusal or escalation path, and red-team testing for prompt manipulation.

addressed_by.covers: uncertainty indicators on outputs
clinical review of high-risk AI outputs

risks.description: There is no documented risk management step for hallucination as a foreseeable misuse or error risk to older adults' health, and no testing against defined metrics before release.
risks.quote: The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Add hallucination hazards to a lifecycle risk register with severity, mitigations and residual-risk acceptance. Link the safeguards in NFR-3.4 to that register and re-assess after each model or knowledge-base update.

addressed_by.covers: post-deployment reporting of incorrect or unsafe AI advice as input to risk identification

recommendations: Define measurable hallucination and accuracy metrics, thresholds and test methods in NFR-3.4, and declare them in the technical documentation.
Specify concrete safeguards in NFR-3.4: grounding with citations, rule-based validation of medication outputs, a low-confidence fallback, and red-team testing.
Establish a lifecycle risk management process that covers hallucination hazards, mitigations and residual risk, and reassess it on each model update.

requirement_text: The app shall provide clear emergency instructions when urgent symptoms are detected.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.5 requires emergency instructions on urgent symptom detection but sets no accuracy, robustness or fail-safe expectations for the detection that triggers them, and no measure of whether users can follow the instructions. A missed or false detection could delay care for vulnerable older adults.

risks.description: The detection that triggers emergency instructions (FR-4.3 urgency classification, FR-7.5 keyword/severe symptom detection) has no declared accuracy metrics, false-negative targets, or robustness requirements, and the instructions themselves have no fail-safe behaviour (e.g. when the AI is unavailable or uncertain).
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define and validate sensitivity/false-negative thresholds for urgent and emergency detection, specify a default-to-emergency-guidance behaviour on low confidence or failure, and test with representative older-adult inputs.

addressed_by.covers: availability of critical health features (partial robustness)
emergency information stays accessible during service disruption

risks.description: The requirement says 'clear' instructions but does not require that users be told the instructions come from an automated detection, or its limits, so older adults may over-rely on or misinterpret the output.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately.
risks.engineering_action: State in the requirement that emergency messages indicate they are AI-triggered, give the reason (triggering symptom), and carry a short limitation note.

addressed_by.covers: explains why important alerts or recommendations were generated
identifies whether advice came from AI, caregiver, or professional

recommendations: Add measurable detection performance targets (false-negative rate) and fail-safe behaviour for urgent-symptom detection and instruction delivery.
Make emergency messages state they are AI-triggered, name the triggering symptom, and include a limitation note, referencing NFR-15.1 and NFR-15.3.

requirement_text: The app shall log AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.6 logs AI advice but does not say what is captured (inputs, model version, confidence, user actions), how long logs are kept, or how they are protected. Without this, events relevant to risk and post-market monitoring cannot be traced, and the logs may fall short of Article 12 and 19 expectations for a likely high-risk health system.

risks.description: The requirement logs only the 'advice' output and does not specify capturing inputs, model/version, confidence, and user/clinician responses. Events relevant to risk situations, substantial modifications and post-market monitoring therefore cannot be traced.
risks.quote: the logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for identifying situations that may result in the AI system presenting a risk
risks.engineering_action: Define a log schema: timestamp, pseudonymised user ID, input context, model/version, output, confidence/uncertainty, urgency class, safety-filter triggers, and user or clinician action (dismiss, challenge, escalate). Link entries to the reports in FR-14.2.

addressed_by.covers: maintaining records needed for clinical safety audits (general record retention, not AI-event-specific)

risks.description: No log retention period is specified for the AI advice logs, and none is aligned with the minimum six months for deployer-held logs or with data-minimisation and deletion requirements.
risks.quote: A provider of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems, to the extent such logs are under their control.
risks.engineering_action: Set a retention period of at least six months, or longer where clinical or medical-device rules require it. Reconcile it with the deletion policy in NFR-13.5 and the health-data privacy rules, and document the legal basis.

addressed_by.covers: data retention and deletion policies (generic, not tied to AI log retention)

risks.description: No requirement states that logs are protected against tampering or restricted to authorised reviewers, even though the logs contain sensitive health data.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Make the AI advice logs append-only and tamper-evident, and restrict access to authorised audit and safety roles. Extend the access auditing in NFR-5.5 to cover them.

addressed_by.covers: audit logs for access to sensitive information
role-based access control

recommendations: Specify the AI log schema, covering inputs, model version, outputs, confidence and user actions.
Define the log retention period and reconcile it with the deletion policy.
Make the logs tamper-evident and restrict access to authorised audit and safety roles.

requirement_text: The app shall obtain user consent before collecting, storing, or sharing health information.

assessment.summary: NFR-4.2 is a consent control for health data, and consent is largely a GDPR matter rather than an AI Act obligation. The only AI Act gap that remains is that consent is not tied to the use of health data for AI model training or improvement, where Article 10 data governance applies.

risks.description: Consent covers collecting, storing, and sharing health data but does not cover use of that data for AI training, validation, or personalisation. Special-category data used for bias monitoring or model improvement therefore has no purpose-specific consent or documented data-governance basis.
risks.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Extend the consent wording to cover AI model training, improvement, and personalisation as a separate, revocable purpose. Record the consent basis in data-governance documentation, and exclude non-consenting users' data from training sets.

addressed_by.covers: anonymisation or de-identification of data used for model improvement, which is part of the data-governance practices in Article 10(2)
consent management features that could record per-purpose consent

recommendations: Add AI training and model-improvement use as a separate consent purpose in NFR-4.2, link it to NFR-13.4 consent records and NFR-4.6 de-identification, and document the basis in data-governance records.

requirement_text: The app shall allow users to view, edit, export, or delete their personal data.

assessment.summary: NFR-4.3 is a data-subject rights control (GDPR-type) and largely not an EU AI Act obligation. The one remaining AI-Act-relevant gap is that edit/delete of personal data is not tied to AI-derived data and logs, so inferred data and training or audit datasets may be left out.

risks.description: Edit/delete/export is not stated to cover AI-inferred data (e.g., mood or loneliness inferences, urgency classifications) or its propagation to training datasets. This may conflict with data governance practices and leave inaccurate inferences uncorrected.
risks.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Clarify that 'personal data' includes AI-inferred attributes. Define how deletion/correction interacts with model-improvement datasets and with retained AI-advice logs (NFR-3.6), and document the retention rules and exceptions.

addressed_by.covers: anonymisation or de-identification of data used for model improvement (data management practice under 10(2))
distinguishes confirmed user data from AI-inferred information, so inferred data can be identified

recommendations: Extend NFR-4.3 to cover AI-inferred data, and specify how deletion and correction interact with training data and audit logs (NFR-3.6), documenting any retention exceptions.

requirement_text: The app shall anonymise or de-identify data where used for analytics or model improvement.

assessment.summary: The requirement commits to anonymising or de-identifying data used for analytics or model improvement, but gives no standard, re-identification testing or data-quality checks for the data reused to improve models. Health data of older adults is special-category data, so weak de-identification could expose individuals, and unvalidated reuse could degrade model quality.

risks.description: The requirement does not define the anonymisation or de-identification standard, nor require re-identification risk testing. 'Anonymise or de-identify' is ambiguous, because pseudonymised health data is still personal data. Re-identification is plausible with rich health, location and demographic records.
risks.quote: the special categories of personal data are subject to technical limitations on a re-use of the personal data, and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
risks.engineering_action: Specify the technique (for example k-anonymity or differential privacy), distinguish anonymised from pseudonymised data, and require documented re-identification risk testing before any dataset is released for analytics or training.

addressed_by.covers: state-of-the-art security measures (encryption in transit and at rest) for sensitive data
data minimisation of health data collected

risks.description: No requirement says that de-identified data reused for model improvement is checked for relevance, representativeness, bias and errors. Stripping identifiers can also remove attributes needed to detect bias against older or vulnerable groups.
risks.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Add data governance steps for datasets derived from user data: provenance records, quality and representativeness checks, and bias examination. Keep the attributes needed for bias testing in a controlled way.

addressed_by.covers: processes for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (output-level only, not training data examination)

risks.description: The requirement does not say that the anonymisation process, the datasets it produces and their use in model improvement are documented as part of the technical documentation.
risks.quote: The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to-date.
risks.engineering_action: Record the de-identification method, the data sources and the training-data handling in the technical documentation, and update it with each model-improvement cycle.

addressed_by.covers: general developer and administrator documentation (not specific to data provenance or training data)

recommendations: Define the anonymisation standard, separate anonymised from pseudonymised data, and require re-identification risk testing before data is released for analytics or training.
Add data governance for datasets derived from user data: provenance, quality, representativeness and bias checks, keeping the attributes needed for bias testing under controlled access.
Document the de-identification pipeline and the training-data practices in the technical documentation and keep them current.

requirement_text: The app shall support secure authentication, such as passwords, PINs, biometrics, or multi-factor authentication.

assessment.summary: NFR-5.2 only says the app 'supports' authentication, listing optional mechanisms ('such as') without requiring any to be enforced or stating a strength. For an AI health app whose AI outputs and health data can be tampered with or accessed by unauthorised parties, this leaves a minor cybersecurity wording gap, since encryption, access control, logging and security testing exist elsewhere in the SRS.

risks.description: The wording is non-binding and non-specific ('support', 'such as'), so no authentication mechanism or strength is mandated (e.g. MFA for caregiver, clinician and administrator roles), which weakens protection against unauthorised access that could alter AI inputs, outputs or user data.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Reword to mandate enforced authentication: require MFA or equivalent for caregiver, clinician and administrator roles, define PIN/password strength and lockout rules, and add the authentication mechanism to security test scope.

addressed_by.covers: role-based access control limiting who can use the system and alter data
protection against unauthorised access to health records
security testing and vulnerability assessments to find exploitable vulnerabilities

recommendations: Make NFR-5.2 a binding, testable requirement: specify which authentication factors are mandatory per role (MFA for non-patient roles), set credential strength and lockout rules, and include them in the NFR-5.7 security test plan.

requirement_text: The app shall maintain audit logs for access to sensitive information.

assessment.summary: NFR-5.5 is a security/privacy control, not an AI-specific function. Its wording is underspecified (which data, which events, retention, tamper-protection), but nearly all AI Act record-keeping obligations are covered by NFR-3.6 and FR-8.6, leaving only a minor clarification gap.

risks.description: The requirement does not define the scope of 'sensitive information', the events logged (e.g. access to AI-inferred health/mood data and AI outputs), log retention, or tamper protection, so it cannot be relied on as evidence of traceability for a high-risk AI system.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: Reword NFR-5.5 to specify the logged events (who, what, when, purpose) for health records and AI-inferred data, tamper-evident storage, and a retention period of at least six months or as required by law.

addressed_by.covers: automatic logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review (Art. 12 traceability of AI outputs)
activity log of caregiver actions

recommendations: Clarify NFR-5.5 to define sensitive data categories, logged access events, tamper protection and retention, and align it with NFR-3.6 and FR-8.6 so AI-related access is traceable.

requirement_text: The app shall use role-based access control for older adults, caregivers, clinicians, and administrators.

assessment.summary: NFR-5.6 sets RBAC for four user groups, which is a sound access control. It does not specify role permissions or tie roles to oversight of high-risk AI outputs, so clinician/administrator access to AI functions is only partly defined. Gaps are narrow because other requirements already cover audit logging, consent-based access and clinical review.

risks.description: Roles are not tied to oversight authority: nothing defines which role (e.g. clinician) may review, override or disregard AI outputs such as symptom urgency classification, or that oversight roles are assigned to competent, authorised persons.
risks.quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Define a role-permission matrix that gives clinicians (and only authorised roles) review, override and reversal rights over AI outputs, and specifies what caregivers and administrators may do with AI settings and outputs.

addressed_by.covers: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs
user can challenge, correct or dismiss AI suggestions

risks.description: RBAC does not state that administrator and clinician privileges over the AI system (model updates, configuration, log access) are restricted and protected against unauthorised alteration.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Specify least-privilege permissions for administrators over model configuration, updates and logs, with MFA and separation of duties for privileged roles.

addressed_by.covers: secure authentication including multi-factor
protection against unauthorised access to health records
security testing and vulnerability assessments

recommendations: Add a role-permission matrix assigning AI review, override and reversal rights to clinicians and defining caregiver and administrator limits.
Specify least-privilege, MFA-protected administrator access to model configuration, updates and logs.

requirement_text: The app shall prevent data loss during crashes or connectivity interruptions.

assessment.summary: NFR-6.4 states a general data-loss prevention goal without scope, measurable targets or resilience mechanisms for AI-related data. For a high-risk health AI system, Article 15 requires declared and verifiable robustness and fault-resilience, which the requirement does not specify.

risks.description: The requirement gives no measurable robustness targets (e.g. recovery point objective, which data is covered, test criteria for crash/connectivity failure), so resilience to faults and inconsistencies cannot be verified or declared. It also does not cover safety-critical data such as symptom entries, medication confirmations or AI-advice logs.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite NFR-6.4 with scope (symptoms, medication confirmations, vitals, AI advice logs, consent changes), a target (e.g. zero acknowledged-entry loss, defined RPO), local persistence with sync/retry and conflict resolution, and fault-injection tests for crashes and connectivity loss. Record the results in the technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: graceful recovery from system errors
continued basic reminders during temporary network issues
offline access to essential information (medication schedules, emergency contacts)
regular backups of user data

risks.description: Nothing ensures that audit and AI-advice logs survive crashes or connectivity interruptions, so records used for safety review and traceability could be lost or left incomplete.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: Extend NFR-6.4 to state explicitly that AI-advice, alert and access logs are durably buffered on the device and synced with integrity checks after a crash or reconnect.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review
audit logs for access to sensitive information

recommendations: Make NFR-6.4 measurable: define covered data, recovery point and recovery time targets, and fault-injection acceptance tests, and document results in the technical documentation.
Explicitly require crash-safe, integrity-checked buffering and sync of AI-advice and audit logs.

requirement_text: The app shall respond quickly to user interactions.

assessment.summary: NFR-7.2 is a generic UI responsiveness requirement with no direct EU AI Act obligation. Related performance concerns, such as AI response time and emergency availability, are handled by NFR-7.3, NFR-6.1 and NFR-14.5.

requirement_text: The AI assistant shall provide responses within an acceptable timeframe.

assessment.summary: The requirement sets a vague, unmeasurable response-time expectation for the AI assistant. Without defined latency targets, performance cannot be verified or declared, and slow responses on urgent symptom queries could delay safety escalation. The gap is mainly one of testability and clarity, not a missing legal control.

risks.description: "Acceptable timeframe" is undefined, so no measurable latency target exists for the assistant's responses, including urgent-symptom and emergency-keyword scenarios, and performance cannot be tested or declared as part of the system's accuracy and robustness levels.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define quantified latency targets (e.g. p95 response time per interaction type, with a stricter bound for urgent/emergency flows), a fallback behaviour when exceeded, and include them in performance testing and technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: scaling of AI services during peak usage to sustain performance
graceful recovery from system errors

recommendations: Replace "acceptable timeframe" with measurable latency thresholds per interaction type (stricter for urgent symptom/emergency flows), define fallback behaviour on timeout, and verify them in performance tests documented in the technical file.

requirement_text: The app shall support offline access to essential information such as medication schedules and emergency contacts.

assessment.summary: Offline access to medication schedules and emergency contacts is an availability and resilience feature, not an AI function. It is largely covered by NFR-6.2, NFR-14.5 and NFR-6.4. The only AI Act-relevant gap is that offline cached data is not protected or checked for staleness, which matters for the robustness and cybersecurity of a likely high-risk health system.

risks.description: Offline cache of sensitive health data (medications, emergency contacts) has no stated integrity, confidentiality or staleness controls, so tampered or outdated schedules could be shown without the user knowing.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: State that offline data is stored encrypted on the device, is integrity-checked, and shows a 'last synced' timestamp. Define how offline edits are reconciled on reconnection.

addressed_by.covers: encryption of sensitive data at rest and in transit
showing users when data was last updated

recommendations: Amend NFR-7.6 to require encrypted, integrity-protected offline storage with a visible last-sync indicator and defined conflict resolution after reconnecting.

requirement_text: The app shall regularly update its medical knowledge base.

assessment.summary: NFR-8.5 requires regular knowledge base updates but gives no cadence, source vetting, validation or re-testing before release. A changed knowledge base can alter AI health outputs and degrade accuracy or introduce unsafe advice, and the change is not controlled.

risks.description: Knowledge base updates are not tied to pre-release validation or re-testing of accuracy and performance, so an update could silently degrade a health-advice system that is likely high-risk (e.g. emergency triage/urgency classification).
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define update cadence and require regression testing against accuracy metrics on a clinical test set, with acceptance thresholds and rollback, before each knowledge base release.

addressed_by.covers: recommendations based on reliable medical knowledge sources (lifecycle accuracy of content)
correction or removal of inaccurate recommendations once identified

risks.description: Update process, source provenance and quality criteria for the knowledge base are unspecified, so content used to ground AI outputs is not governed (source selection, currency, errors, bias).
risks.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose of the AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Document approved sources, provenance, review by clinical staff, versioning and bias/representativeness checks for knowledge base content, applied on each update.

addressed_by.covers: use of reliable medical knowledge sources

risks.description: Knowledge base changes are not required to be versioned or documented, so substantial changes to system behaviour are not traceable in technical documentation or the post-market and change-management process.
risks.quote: The technical documentation of a high-risk AI system shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date.
risks.engineering_action: Require a versioned changelog of each knowledge base update, linked to the technical documentation and to a change assessment for whether it is a substantial modification.

addressed_by.covers: clear documentation for developers and administrators

recommendations: Specify update frequency and require regression testing with acceptance thresholds and rollback before releasing each knowledge base update.
Define source vetting, provenance, clinical review and bias checks for knowledge base content.
Version every knowledge base update and record it in technical documentation, with an assessment of whether it is a substantial modification.

requirement_text: The system shall support regular software updates and bug fixes.

assessment.summary: NFR-9.3 commits to regular updates and bug fixes but sets no governance over them. For an AI health system that is plausibly high-risk (symptom urgency classification, emergency detection), updates that alter AI behaviour could occur with no re-validation, change documentation or substantial-modification assessment, and no vulnerability or accuracy safeguards.

risks.description: Updates and bug fixes have no change-control requirement for re-assessing risk, re-testing accuracy, or deciding whether a change is a substantial modification needing a new conformity assessment.
risks.quote: For high-risk AI systems that have already been subject to a conformity assessment procedure, in the event of a substantial modification, the new conformity assessment procedure shall be carried out
risks.engineering_action: Add a release-governance step that classifies each update as AI-affecting or not, flags potential substantial modifications, and triggers re-assessment and a documented decision. Define in technical documentation which changes are pre-determined.

addressed_by.covers: module-level testing of reminders, AI assistant, notifications and data sharing before release

risks.description: Regular updates are not tied to maintaining accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity over the lifecycle, including patching vulnerabilities and preventing regressions in AI behaviour.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Require regression tests against declared accuracy and robustness metrics and security patch SLAs as release gates for every update, with rollback.

addressed_by.covers: regular security testing and vulnerability assessments
testing of individual modules

risks.description: Updates and fixes are not required to be recorded in the technical documentation or version history, so the documentation may drift from the deployed system.
risks.quote: The technical documentation shall be drawn up in such a way as to demonstrate that the high-risk AI system complies with the requirements set out in this Section
risks.engineering_action: Require each release to update versioned technical documentation and a changelog covering changes to AI components, with retention for the required period.

addressed_by.covers: maintaining documentation for developers and administrators

risks.description: Bug reports and incident findings from users and operations are not linked to the update process as post-market monitoring inputs.
risks.quote: Providers shall establish and document a post-market monitoring system in a manner that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Feed unsafe-advice reports and monitoring data into a documented corrective-action and update workflow with traceability from issue to release.

addressed_by.covers: users reporting incorrect or unsafe AI advice
correcting or removing inaccurate recommendations once identified

recommendations: Add change control that flags AI-affecting updates and potential substantial modifications for conformity re-assessment.
Make accuracy and robustness regression tests, security patching and rollback release gates.
Version the technical documentation and changelog with every release.
Link bug and incident reports to a documented corrective-action and update workflow.

requirement_text: The system shall allow older adults to create an account using email, phone number, or caregiver-assisted registration.

assessment.summary: FR-1.1 is an account-creation function (email, phone, caregiver-assisted registration) and does not itself perform any high-risk AI function. No requirement-level gap is attributable to the EU AI Act provisions supplied.

requirement_text: The system shall support different user roles, including older adult, caregiver, doctor, nurse, and administrator.

assessment.summary: FR-1.5 only defines user role types (older adult, caregiver, doctor, nurse, administrator). It is an access and identity function and does not itself impose an AI Act obligation. Role-based access control and access protection are covered elsewhere in the SRS (NFR-5.6, NFR-5.4, NFR-5.5).

requirement_text: The system shall provide access to mental health helplines or support resources.

assessment.summary: FR-10.4 only provides access to helplines or support resources. It is a supportive safeguard and not itself a high-risk function. No provision in the supplied Act text imposes a requirement-level gap on it.

requirement_text: The system shall generate personalised health reminders based on the user’s age, health conditions, medication schedule, and activity patterns.

assessment.summary: FR-11.1 drives medication- and health-related reminders from age, conditions and activity patterns, but states no accuracy, bias-mitigation or risk-treatment expectations. The SRS also leaves open whether this function is a high-risk system (medical device route), so the compliance scope is uncertain. This is engineering review support, not legal advice.

risks.description: No declared accuracy or correctness metrics for personalised reminders. A wrong or missed medication or health reminder can cause harm to older adults, and the SRS defines no measurable target or declaration in the instructions for use.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Define accuracy and robustness metrics for reminder personalisation (for example, correct timing against the medication schedule and correct condition and age rule application). Set acceptance thresholds, test against them before release, and declare them in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: accuracy of reminder scheduling across time zones and daylight saving (partial input to 15(1) accuracy)

risks.description: Personalisation by age and health condition can produce biased or discriminatory reminders, for example under-reminding older or multi-morbid users. The SRS has a bias review process but no bias detection and mitigation measures or data-quality criteria for the data feeding this function.
risks.quote: examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations
risks.engineering_action: Specify bias examination of the personalisation logic and its data (age, condition and activity-pattern inputs) across subgroups. Define mitigation measures and acceptance criteria, and document data representativeness and completeness for the intended older-adult population.

addressed_by.covers: process for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (examination step of 10(2)(f), without mitigation)
design intent to avoid ageist assumptions

risks.description: No risk management process covers hazards of this function, such as wrong dose or timing prompts, alarm fatigue, or misuse by cognitively impaired users. The adverse impact on older adults as a vulnerable group is not considered.
risks.quote: providers shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups.
risks.engineering_action: Establish a documented, iterative risk management process that covers reminder hazards, including vulnerable-user considerations for older adults. Define targeted mitigations and residual-risk acceptance, and test against predefined metrics before release.

risks.description: The SRS does not decide whether personalised health reminders fall under the high-risk regime, for example as medical device software under Annex I. NFR-13.2 only conditionally mentions medical software regulation, so it is unclear which Chapter III obligations apply to this requirement.
risks.quote: that AI system shall be considered to be high-risk where both of the following conditions are fulfilled
risks.engineering_action: Document an intended-purpose and classification assessment, covering medical device qualification and third-party conformity assessment, for the reminder function. Record the outcome in the technical documentation and trace Chapter III obligations to this requirement if it is high-risk.

addressed_by.covers: conditional compliance with medical software regulation (does not decide classification)

recommendations: Define and declare accuracy and robustness metrics with acceptance thresholds for reminder personalisation.
Add bias detection, mitigation and data-quality criteria for age, condition and activity inputs, extending NFR-12.7.
Establish a risk management process for reminder hazards that explicitly considers older adults as a vulnerable group.
Document the high-risk classification and medical-device qualification of the reminder function and trace the resulting obligations.

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to customise notification frequency and style.

assessment.summary: FR-12.2 is a user-preference feature for notification frequency and style. It performs no AI inference and makes no decision about a person, so none of the supplied provisions imposes a requirement-level gap on its wording.

requirement_text: The system shall avoid excessive notifications to reduce confusion or alarm.

assessment.summary: FR-12.5 is a UX goal to limit notification volume. It has no EU AI Act obligation of its own, and no cited provision supports a requirement-level gap. Existing requirements (FR-12.2, FR-12.4) already cover customisation and critical-reminder repetition.

requirement_text: The system shall highlight important changes, missed medications, abnormal readings, or recurring symptoms.

assessment.summary: FR-13.5 leaves the detection and highlighting of abnormal readings, missed medications and recurring symptoms undefined. It has no accuracy or robustness targets, no risk analysis of missed or false flags for older adults, and no instructions-for-use content on how to interpret the highlights. This matters if the system is high-risk, for example as medical-device software (Annex I) or triage-type functionality. That classification is not settled in the SRS.

risks.description: The criteria for 'important', 'abnormal' and 'recurring' are not defined, and no accuracy or robustness levels or metrics (sensitivity to missed abnormal readings, false-alarm rate) are specified or declared, so missed flags could go undetected.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define thresholds and detection logic for each highlight type (clinically sourced, per-user baseline). Set target sensitivity/specificity with acceptance criteria. Test against them before release, monitor them in operation, and declare the metrics in the instructions for use (Art. 15(3)).

risks.description: No risk management covers the harms of this function: false negatives that give false reassurance, false positives that cause alarm or alert fatigue, and the vulnerability of older users or those with cognitive impairment.
risks.quote: the estimation and evaluation of the risks that may emerge when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose, and under conditions of reasonably foreseeable misuse;
risks.engineering_action: Add the highlighting function to the hazard analysis. Cover missed-alert and false-alert scenarios and effects on vulnerable users (Art. 9(9)). Define mitigations and residual-risk acceptance criteria, and test against predefined metrics before release (Art. 9(8)).

risks.description: The instructions for use do not yet have to describe what the highlights mean, their limitations and the conditions that degrade their accuracy, so deployers and caregivers may misread the highlighted output.
risks.quote: the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance of the high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Document in the instructions for use how each highlight is generated, its known limits (such as sparse data or sensor error) and how caregivers and clinicians should interpret it. Show the triggering data and basis with each highlight.

addressed_by.covers: explains to users why important alerts or recommendations were generated, supporting interpretation of the output (13(1))
confidence or uncertainty indicators that support appropriate use of the output (13(1))

recommendations: Define clinically sourced detection criteria and declared accuracy metrics for each highlight type, and test against them before release.
Add missed-flag, false-flag and alert-fatigue hazards, including vulnerable-user effects, to the risk management system with acceptance criteria.
Document the meaning and limits of each highlight in the instructions for use, and show the triggering data and basis with each highlight.

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to provide feedback about app usability and AI responses.

assessment.summary: FR-14.1 is a feedback channel and is not itself a compliance problem. If the symptom-urgency triage (FR-4.3) makes the system high-risk under Annex III 5(d), the requirement does not say that feedback is documented and analysed as post-market performance data, so it may not feed the monitoring Article 72 requires.

risks.description: The requirement only lets users submit feedback. It does not say the feedback is stored, linked to the AI output concerned, and analysed within a post-market monitoring plan to check continued compliance. FR-14.2 collects reports of unsafe AI advice, but that is a narrower input.
risks.quote: The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime
risks.engineering_action: State that feedback is stored with a reference to the AI response, categorised (usability / accuracy / safety), and routed into the post-market monitoring plan with periodic review and escalation criteria for possible serious incidents. Confirm the Annex III 5(d) classification of the triage function (FR-4.3).

addressed_by.covers: collection of user reports of incorrect or unsafe AI advice, one source of performance data under 72(2)

recommendations: Extend FR-14.1 so feedback is recorded against the specific AI response and fed into the documented post-market monitoring plan with defined review cadence and escalation, and confirm whether the triage function is high-risk under Annex III 5(d).

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to report incorrect or unsafe AI advice.

assessment.summary: FR-14.2 gives users a way to report incorrect or unsafe AI advice, but it does not say where the reports go. Without routing into post-market monitoring and serious-incident handling, reports of harmful advice may never reach the provider, and legal reporting deadlines could be missed. This assumes the system falls in a high-risk category, for example emergency healthcare triage under Annex III 5(d) or a medical device; confirm that classification.

risks.description: User reports are not specified as an input to a documented post-market monitoring system that collects, documents and analyses performance data and evaluates continuous compliance, so the reporting channel could stay an isolated feedback form.
risks.quote: The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime
risks.engineering_action: State that each report is stored as a structured record (advice ID, user context, category, severity). Feed these records into the post-market monitoring plan with defined analysis and review cadence.

addressed_by.covers: documenting AI-generated advice for safety review, which gives report records the advice they refer to

risks.description: The requirement has no severity triage or escalation path, so a report describing harm from AI advice (injury, delayed emergency care) cannot be routed to the provider's serious-incident procedure within the 15-, 10- or 2-day deadlines.
risks.quote: The report referred to in paragraph 1 shall be made immediately after the provider has established a causal link between the AI system and the serious incident or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and, in any event, not later than 15 days after the provider or, where applicable, the deployer, becomes aware of the serious incident.
risks.engineering_action: Add a 'harm occurred' flag and severity classification to the report form. Automatically escalate suspected serious incidents to a named compliance owner, with timestamped awareness date and a link to the incident-reporting and investigation workflow.

recommendations: Route every FR-14.2 report into a post-market monitoring dataset with defined analysis and periodic review, and link it to the AI advice log.
Add severity triage to the report flow and escalate suspected serious incidents to a documented Article 73 reporting procedure with deadline tracking.

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to confirm whether they have taken, skipped, or delayed a medication.

assessment.summary: FR-2.3 is a simple user-entered adherence log (taken/skipped/delayed). It is not an AI function, so no EU AI Act obligation attaches to the requirement itself. The only residual concern is that the adherence data may feed downstream AI features (FR-2.4, FR-4.6, FR-11.3), which should carry the relevant obligations.

requirement_text: The system shall provide an AI-powered virtual assistant that can answer general health-related questions in simple language.

assessment.summary: FR-3.1 introduces a generative, user-facing health chatbot but does not say users are told they are talking to an AI, and nothing in the SRS requires machine-readable marking of its generated text.
