This leaves Article 50 transparency obligations only partly met. Annex III does not list general health Q&A, so no high-risk obligations are raised here.

risks.description: The assistant generates synthetic text, but no requirement in the SRS makes its outputs machine-readable and detectable as AI-generated.
risks.quote: Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
risks.engineering_action: Add a requirement that assistant outputs carry machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. metadata or watermark in API and export payloads). Check the technical solution is robust and interoperable, and document any applicable exemption.

risks.description: The requirement does not state that users are informed at first interaction that they are talking to an AI. Existing requirements label advice and recommendations as AI-generated but do not cover a clear up-front interaction notice.
risks.quote: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system
risks.engineering_action: Amend FR-3.1 to require a clear, accessible disclosure (text and voice) that the user is talking to an AI, shown at or before the first interaction in every session channel.

addressed_by.covers: identifies whether advice came from AI, a caregiver or a professional
indicates when recommendations are AI-generated

recommendations: Add machine-readable marking of AI-generated assistant text, with documented robustness, or record why an exemption applies.
Reword FR-3.1 to require an explicit AI-interaction disclosure at first interaction, usable by voice and text and meeting accessibility needs.

requirement_text: The system shall provide health guidance based on the user’s profile, symptoms, and history where appropriate.

assessment.summary: FR-3.3 generates personalised health guidance from profile, symptom and history data for older adults, but it names no risk management process, no accuracy target or declared metrics, and no data-quality or representativeness criteria. If the system is high-risk (for example as medical device software under Art. 6(1), which NFR-13.2 hints at), these gaps would block conformity assessment and could harm a vulnerable user group.

risks.description: No lifecycle risk management process identifies, evaluates and mitigates risks from personalised health guidance (unsafe or inappropriate advice, effects on older and vulnerable users). The existing NFRs are individual safeguards, not a documented iterative process.
risks.quote: The risk management system shall be understood as a continuous iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of a high-risk AI system, requiring regular systematic review and updating.
risks.engineering_action: Establish a documented risk management process for the guidance feature. It should cover hazard identification (including foreseeable misuse and the older-adult user group), risk evaluation, mitigation, residual-risk acceptance and post-market feedback (e.g. from FR-14.2 reports). Link existing safeguards (NFR-3.3, NFR-3.4) to identified risks.

addressed_by.covers: a mitigation measure against unsafe or unsupported recommendations (9(2)(d)), not a risk management process
a mitigation measure against hallucinated medical advice (9(2)(d)), not a risk management process

risks.description: The requirement sets no accuracy target or metrics for the personalised guidance. Nothing says accuracy levels will be declared in the instructions for use. Confidence indicators alone are not accuracy metrics.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Define accuracy and robustness metrics and acceptance thresholds for the guidance (e.g. clinical concordance, unsafe-advice rate, by age and condition subgroup). Test against them before release and declare the results in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: uncertainty indicators for individual outputs, not declared accuracy levels or metrics

risks.description: Personalisation from profile and history lacks data-governance criteria. These cover representativeness of the data for older adults, data gaps, and bias examination and mitigation in the data behind the guidance. The SRS has only a general bias-review process.
risks.quote: examination in view of possible biases that are likely to affect the health and safety of persons, have a negative impact on fundamental rights or lead to discrimination prohibited under Union law, especially where data outputs influence inputs for future operations;
risks.engineering_action: Document data governance for the training, validation and testing data and the knowledge sources. Cover provenance, representativeness across age, sex and comorbidity groups, gap identification, and bias detection and mitigation with acceptance criteria. Include the feedback loop where past behaviour and history shape later guidance (FR-11.3).

addressed_by.covers: a process for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (10(2)(f)), without data-set quality criteria or mitigation measures

risks.description: Nothing addresses automation bias or over-reliance by older users or overseers on personalised guidance. Disclaimers and challenge options exist, but no measure helps overseers recognise and counter over-reliance.
risks.quote: to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias)
risks.engineering_action: Add oversight design for the guidance feature. Include in-context cues against over-reliance, guidance to clinical reviewers and caregivers on automation bias, and escalation criteria for human review of guidance.

recommendations: Establish a documented, iterative risk management process covering the guidance feature, with older adults as an explicit vulnerable group.
Define, test and declare accuracy metrics and thresholds for personalised guidance, including subgroup performance, in the instructions for use.
Add data governance for the personalisation data and knowledge sources, covering representativeness, gaps and bias mitigation with acceptance criteria.
Add automation-bias safeguards and escalation criteria so overseers and users do not over-rely on AI guidance.
Confirm the high-risk classification (Art. 6(1) via medical device rules, or Annex III) and document the outcome, since these obligations depend on it.

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to record symptoms such as pain, dizziness, shortness of breath, fatigue, fever, or confusion.

assessment.summary: FR-4.1 only captures user-entered symptoms. It is a data-entry function that makes no decision, classification or recommendation, so no requirement-level gap arises under the supplied provisions. The high-risk questions (urgency triage, Annex III 5(d) and medical-device status) belong to FR-4.3, FR-4.4 and FR-7.5, not to this requirement.

requirement_text: The system shall ask follow-up questions to better understand reported symptoms.

assessment.summary: FR-4.2 adds an interactive question step to symptom intake and triage, which is likely high-risk (emergency healthcare triage, Annex III 5(d), or medical-device functionality). The requirement does not address vulnerable older users, such as those who are confused or have impaired cognition, or how question quality is measured, and it does not say whether follow-up exchanges are logged. Existing escalation and safeguard requirements cover only part of this.

risks.description: The follow-up question flow has no defined risk analysis for foreseeable misuse or vulnerable users (cognitively impaired or confused older adults, misunderstood questions, wrong answers), and there are no stop or escalation criteria tied to the questioning itself. This could lead to missed red flags or wrong urgency classification.
risks.quote: providers shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups.
risks.engineering_action: Add a risk analysis for the questioning flow covering vulnerable users and misinterpretation. Define rules such as a maximum question count, immediate escalation on red-flag answers, and a fallback to human assistance when answers are inconsistent or indicate confusion.

addressed_by.covers: escalation of potentially serious symptoms to emergency or professional care guidance (a risk mitigation measure under 9(2)(d))
detection of emergency keywords or severe symptoms and recommendation of urgent action

risks.description: No accuracy or robustness metrics are specified for the question-and-answer step that feeds urgency classification, for example whether follow-up questions improve triage accuracy for older users or handle ambiguous or voice-transcribed answers. Such metrics would need to be declared in the instructions for use.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Define accuracy and robustness metrics and acceptance thresholds for symptom elicitation and triage, including performance across age and cognitive-ability subgroups and voice input. Test against them before release and declare them in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: confidence or uncertainty indicators shown to users (does not declare accuracy levels or metrics)

risks.description: It is unspecified whether the questions asked and the user's answers are automatically recorded, so the questioning steps behind a triage outcome may not be traceable for incident analysis or post-market monitoring.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
risks.engineering_action: State in FR-4.2 that each generated follow-up question and the user's response are logged, linked to the resulting urgency classification and recommendation, and retained per the log retention policy.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review

recommendations: Add a risk analysis and escalation rules for the follow-up questioning flow, covering vulnerable and cognitively impaired users.
Define and test accuracy and robustness metrics for the symptom-elicitation and triage pipeline, and declare them in the instructions for use.
Log each follow-up question and answer, linked to the triage outcome, and apply the log retention policy.

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to store appointment details such as doctor name, clinic location, reason for visit, and preparation notes.

assessment.summary: FR-6.3 is a plain data-storage function for appointment details. It involves no AI inference, classification or decision-making, and no supplied provision imposes a requirement-level obligation on it.

requirement_text: The system shall provide a clearly visible emergency assistance button.

assessment.summary: FR-7.1 is a plain UI requirement (a visible emergency assistance button) with no AI decision-making of its own. No requirement-level EU AI Act gap follows from the button; emergency AI detection and triage sit in other requirements (e.g., FR-7.5, FR-4.3).

requirement_text: The system shall allow caregivers to send reminders or supportive messages to the older adult.

assessment.summary: FR-8.4 is a simple caregiver-to-older-adult messaging feature. It performs no inference, profiling or decision-making, so it is not a high-risk function under Annex III and no requirement-level gap is supported by the supplied provisions.

requirement_text: The system shall maintain an activity log of caregiver actions for transparency.

assessment.summary: FR-8.6 logs caregiver actions 'for transparency' but does not say which events are recorded, that recording is automatic, or how long logs are kept. If the system is classed as high-risk (for example as medical-device software), the log would not clearly support traceability or retention duties. This is engineering review support, not legal advice.

risks.description: The log is framed as caregiver transparency and does not state that it automatically records events relevant to identifying risk situations, post-market monitoring, or deployer monitoring (e.g. caregiver overrides of medication schedules or alert handling that feed AI-driven outputs).
risks.quote: logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for: (a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification; (b) facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72; and (c) monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5).
risks.engineering_action: Define the logged event schema (actor, action, timestamp, affected user, linked AI output or alert ID). State that logging is automatic and tamper-evident, and link caregiver actions to the AI-generated outputs they act on. Document the high-risk classification decision so the scope of Article 12 is clear.

addressed_by.covers: automatic recording of AI-generated advice events for audit and safety review (12(1), 12(2))

risks.description: No retention period is set for the caregiver activity log, so it may be deleted before the minimum period expected for high-risk systems, or conflict with the deletion policies in NFR-13.5.
risks.quote: the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
risks.engineering_action: Add a retention rule of at least six months, or longer if the intended purpose requires it. Reconcile it with the data deletion and privacy requirements, using pseudonymised log entries where the user requests deletion.

recommendations: Specify the caregiver log's event schema, automatic capture, integrity protection, and its links to AI outputs and alerts, and document the system's high-risk classification.
Add a minimum six-month retention requirement for the log and reconcile it with the deletion policies in NFR-13.5.

requirement_text: The app shall use a simple and intuitive interface suitable for older adults.

assessment.summary: NFR-1.1 is a general usability requirement for older adults. No AI Act provision imposes a gap on this wording, and accessibility and human-oversight interface concerns are covered by other requirements.

requirement_text: The app shall support guided onboarding for first-time users.

assessment.summary: NFR-1.6 (guided onboarding for first-time users) is a usability requirement. It does not itself implement or conflict with any AI Act obligation, and no supplied provision requires a gap-fill in this wording.

requirement_text: The system shall support an increasing number of users without major performance degradation.

assessment.summary: NFR-10.1 is a generic scalability requirement with no AI-specific obligation. The only link to the Act is performance consistency under load, which is not specified here and is partly covered elsewhere.

requirement_text: The system shall support scaling of AI services during peak usage.

assessment.summary: NFR-10.2 is a generic scalability requirement and does not by itself create a requirement-level EU AI Act gap. Robustness and performance consistency under peak load are covered by other SRS items, and no listed provision requires a change to this wording.

requirement_text: The app shall support integration with common wearable devices and health monitoring tools.

assessment.summary: NFR-11.1 only says the app must integrate with wearables and health monitoring tools. It sets no data validation, integrity or compatibility conditions for third-party device inputs, so erroneous or manipulated readings could drive health alerts and recommendations. This matters if the system is high-risk (for example as a medical device function or emergency triage), which the SRS does not settle.

risks.description: No requirement for plausibility checks, error handling or fail-safe behaviour when wearable data is faulty, missing, drifting or inconsistent, which could distort symptom urgency or abnormal-reading alerts.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates, in particular due to their interaction with natural persons or other systems.
risks.engineering_action: Extend the requirement with input validation (range, plausibility, timestamp and sensor-quality checks), handling of device outages or conflicting readings, and rules that low-quality device data lowers confidence or is excluded from AI-driven alerts.

risks.description: Third-party device and tool integrations are an external input channel, but no device authentication, data-origin integrity or defence against spoofed or manipulated readings is specified.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Require authenticated, integrity-protected device pairing and data ingestion (signed or authenticated payloads, source allow-listing, anomaly detection on ingested data). Include integration endpoints in threat modelling and security testing.

risks.description: The requirement says 'common' devices and tools without defining supported devices, data types or input specifications, so deployers cannot be told what input data the AI expects or how device quality affects accuracy.
risks.quote: when appropriate, specifications for the input data
risks.engineering_action: Define a supported-device and data-format list and document input specifications and known accuracy limitations per device class in the instructions for use.

recommendations: Add input validation, plausibility checks and degraded-mode behaviour for wearable data feeding AI features.
Require authenticated, integrity-protected device integrations and cover them in security testing.
Specify supported devices and input data specifications and document their accuracy limitations in the instructions for use.

requirement_text: The app shall respect user autonomy and allow older adults to make their own decisions where possible.

assessment.summary: NFR-12.2 is a high-level autonomy statement with no testable criteria. NFR-15.4 already provides the dismiss/correct control, so the remaining gap is small: nothing addresses over-reliance (automation bias) among older adult users, and 'where possible' leaves the override scope undefined. This assumes the AI triage and symptom-urgency functions bring the system into high-risk scope, which should be confirmed.

risks.description: The requirement does not address users' tendency to over-rely on AI output (automation bias), which is a particular risk for older adults receiving symptom-urgency and health recommendations.
risks.quote: to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias)
risks.engineering_action: Add acceptance criteria for automation-bias mitigation, such as periodic in-app prompts to verify AI advice, no default-accept patterns, and usability testing with older adults for over-reliance. Document these in the instructions for use.

risks.description: 'Where possible' leaves unspecified which AI outputs the user can decide not to use or override. The existing control in NFR-15.4 covers dismissal of suggestions but not, for example, urgency classifications or caregiver alerts.
risks.quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system
risks.engineering_action: Reword the requirement to enumerate the AI outputs the user can disregard or override (urgency classification, recommendations, mood detection, caregiver alerts). State the safety-critical exceptions explicitly and cross-reference NFR-15.4.

addressed_by.covers: users can challenge, correct, or dismiss AI-generated suggestions (14(4)(d))

recommendations: Add testable automation-bias mitigations and evaluate over-reliance in usability testing with older adults.
Rewrite NFR-12.2 to list the AI outputs users can override or disregard, with defined safety-critical exceptions, and link it to NFR-15.4.

requirement_text: The app shall clearly distinguish between AI advice and human clinical advice.

assessment.summary: NFR-12.3 supports AI/human labelling, but it does not say when the label must appear or how it reaches older adults on voice or accessibility channels. Other requirements already cover most of the labelling, so the remaining gap is wording clarity.

risks.description: The requirement does not state that users are told they are interacting with an AI system at or before first interaction, in a clear, distinguishable and accessible form (including voice and screen-reader channels).
risks.quote: The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure. The information shall conform to the applicable accessibility requirements.
risks.engineering_action: Reword NFR-12.3 to require an AI-disclosure notice at first use of the assistant and its voice mode. Add a persistent visual and audible AI/human label that meets the accessibility requirements (WCAG, screen reader, voice output).

addressed_by.covers: identifies whether advice came from AI, a caregiver, or a healthcare professional (the source distinction in 50(1))
clearly indicates when recommendations are AI-generated

recommendations: Make NFR-12.3 specify an AI-interaction disclosure at first interaction, delivered through text, voice and assistive-technology channels, and consistent with NFR-15.3 and FR-11.5.

requirement_text: The app shall be designed to support independence, not replace human care.

assessment.summary: NFR-12.5 is a high-level design principle with no verifiable criteria, so it does not by itself implement human oversight or intervention measures. Concrete oversight measures exist in other requirements, but this requirement is not traceable to them.

risks.description: The requirement states a design intent (supporting independence, not replacing human care) without any testable oversight measure, so it cannot demonstrate that natural persons can effectively oversee, disregard, override or halt the AI features (symptom urgency classification, mood and loneliness detection, health guidance).
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite NFR-12.5 into verifiable criteria that reference the concrete oversight controls: AI outputs are advisory only, users can disregard or override them (NFR-15.4), clinicians review high-risk outputs (NFR-8.6), and human assistance is available (FR-14.5). Add acceptance tests, and document these measures in the oversight section of the technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: ability to disregard, challenge or dismiss AI-generated suggestions (14(4)(d))
clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (human oversight measure, 14(3))
no final medical diagnosis without professional clinical review
uncertainty indicators supporting understanding of system limitations (14(4)(a))

recommendations: Make NFR-12.5 testable and trace it to the oversight controls (NFR-15.4, NFR-8.6, FR-3.5, FR-14.5), including a stop/disable mechanism for AI features and guidance on automation bias.

requirement_text: The app shall maintain records needed for clinical safety audits.

assessment.summary: NFR-13.3 requires records for clinical safety audits but does not define which events are logged, their retention period, or their integrity. This leaves Article 12 and 19 logging and traceability obligations only partly specified, although NFR-3.6 and NFR-5.5 cover parts of them.

risks.description: The requirement does not define which events the audit records must capture, such as risk-relevant situations, substantial modifications, post-market monitoring inputs, or deployer monitoring data. 'Records needed for clinical safety audits' is too vague to show the Article 12(2) traceability purposes are met.
risks.quote: logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for:
risks.engineering_action: Specify the event types logged: AI inputs and outputs, model and version, urgency classification, clinician overrides, user challenges and safety reports, and model updates. Map each to Article 12(2)(a)-(c).

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review (partial 12(2) event recording)
capture of user reports of incorrect or unsafe AI advice, a source of risk-relevant events (12(2)(a))

risks.description: The requirement sets no retention period for the records and no integrity or tamper-protection control, so records could be deleted early (for example under NFR-13.5 deletion policies) or altered.
risks.quote: the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
risks.engineering_action: Define a retention period of at least six months, longer where clinical safety needs it. Make the audit records append-only and tamper-evident. Exempt them from user-initiated deletion, or resolve the conflict with data protection law explicitly.

addressed_by.covers: audit logs for access to sensitive information (access logging only, not retention of AI event logs)

recommendations: Define the audit record content, mapped to Article 12(2) purposes, covering AI outputs, model versions, overrides, user challenges and safety reports.
Set a retention period of at least six months and add integrity protection for the records, resolving the conflict with the NFR-13.5 deletion policies.

requirement_text: The system shall maintain regular backups of user data.

assessment.summary: NFR-14.1 only requires regular backups of user data and does not itself engage a specific EU AI Act obligation. Backup and recovery resilience is mostly covered by other requirements (NFR-14.2, NFR-6.4), so no requirement-level gap is identified.

requirement_text: The system shall support disaster recovery procedures.

assessment.summary: NFR-14.2 is a one-line, untestable statement. It sets no recovery objectives, does not cover AI components or fail-safe behaviour, and does not mention preserving the AI logs. If the system is high-risk (for example, medical-device functionality under Annex I), this weakens the Art. 15(4) robustness evidence and the Art. 19 log retention. This is engineering review support, not legal advice.

risks.description: The requirement gives no scope, recovery time/point objectives or fail-safe behaviour for the AI components (symptom urgency classification, assistant, emergency detection) after a disaster, so robustness cannot be verified or documented.
risks.quote: The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite NFR-14.2 to define RTO/RPO per service tier, covering AI inference and model artefacts. Specify the fail-safe state when AI services are down (e.g. suppress urgency classification and show emergency guidance). Require periodic DR tests with documented results for the technical documentation.

addressed_by.covers: backup of user data, part of the backup plans in Art. 15(4)
fail-safe availability of emergency information during disruption
graceful recovery from system errors, supporting resilience to faults

risks.description: Disaster recovery does not state that automatically generated AI and audit logs are backed up and restored, so the log retention period could be broken by a disaster.
risks.quote: Providers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs referred to in Article 12(1), automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems
risks.engineering_action: Add to NFR-14.2 that AI advice logs (NFR-3.6) and audit logs (NFR-5.5) are included in backup and recovery, with integrity checks and retention of at least six months.

recommendations: Make NFR-14.2 measurable: RTO/RPO targets, AI-service scope, defined fail-safe behaviour and a DR test cadence, with results kept in the technical documentation.
Include AI and audit logs in the DR scope, with integrity verification and retention of at least six months.

requirement_text: The system shall notify users of planned maintenance where possible.

assessment.summary: NFR-14.4 only commits to notifying users of planned maintenance 'where possible'. It is an operational availability notice with no AI-specific compliance obligation under the supplied provisions, so no requirement-level gap is identified.

requirement_text: The app shall explain why important alerts or recommendations were generated.

assessment.summary: The requirement gives an end-user explanation feature for alerts and recommendations, but "important" is undefined and the explanation content is not tied to the actual drivers of the output or to the people who oversee it. If the system is high-risk (e.g. symptom urgency triage), this weakens output interpretability under Art. 13/14. The classification itself is not settled by the SRS.

risks.description: Scope and content of the explanation are unspecified: "important" is undefined, and nothing requires the explanation to reflect the real factors behind the output (e.g. urgency classification, anomaly detection, emergency keyword detection). It is also not addressed to caregivers or clinicians who review high-risk outputs.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way as to ensure that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system’s output and use it appropriately.
risks.engineering_action: Define which alert and recommendation types are "important" (urgency classification, pattern-change alerts, emergency recommendations). For each, require an explanation generated from the actual model inputs and features, not post-hoc text. Provide a more detailed view for caregivers and clinicians. Include the explanation capability in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: plain-language explanation of AI-generated suggestions from the assistant (13(3)(b)(iv))
confidence or uncertainty indicators to support interpretation of outputs (13(3)(b)(vii))
identification of the advice source (AI, caregiver or professional)

risks.description: The reviewing person cannot reliably interpret an output or detect over-reliance on it unless the explanation is stored with the alert. The requirement does not say that the explanation or its contributing factors are retained for audit and oversight.
risks.quote: to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system’s output, taking into account, for example, the interpretation tools and methods available;
risks.engineering_action: Store the generated explanation and its contributing factors with each important alert or recommendation. Display them to clinicians or caregivers reviewing high-risk outputs.

addressed_by.covers: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (14(4)(c)-(d) review of output)
logging of AI-generated advice for audit

recommendations: Define which alerts and recommendations count as "important" and require explanations grounded in the actual model drivers, with a deeper view for caregivers and clinicians.
Persist the explanation and contributing factors alongside the logged advice so reviewers can interpret outputs and audit them.

requirement_text: The app shall avoid creating false reassurance when symptoms may require medical attention.

assessment.summary: NFR-15.5 states the right safety goal but gives no measurable criterion, test method or accuracy metric for 'false reassurance'. It also does not address user over-reliance on low-urgency outputs. Symptom urgency classification (FR-4.3) may fall under Annex III 5(d) triage, so under-triage of older adults could cause real harm and the requirement could not be verified at conformity assessment.

risks.description: The requirement is not testable: no under-triage or false-negative metric, threshold or pre-release test protocol is defined for symptoms that need medical attention, and older adults as a vulnerable group are not considered.
risks.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite as a measurable criterion, e.g. maximum under-triage rate for urgent/emergency symptom classes, tested on a representative older-adult symptom set before release and after each model update. Record false reassurance as an identified risk, including its impact on vulnerable users, in the risk management file.

addressed_by.covers: risk management measure: escalation of potentially serious symptoms to care guidance (9(2)(d))
risk management measure: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (9(2)(d))

risks.description: No accuracy or robustness level is specified for urgency classification. Sensitivity for urgent and emergency cases, and consistent performance over the lifecycle, are not defined or declared to deployers.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Define accuracy metrics for urgency classification (per-class sensitivity, under-triage rate, subgroup performance by age and comorbidity). Monitor them across model updates and declare the achieved levels in the instructions for use.

addressed_by.covers: partial: uncertainty indicators on outputs, not declared accuracy levels

risks.description: The requirement does not address the tendency of older users to over-rely on reassuring outputs (automation bias). Nothing makes users aware that a 'no concern' output may be wrong or tells them when to seek care regardless.
risks.quote: to remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output produced by a high-risk AI system (automation bias)
risks.engineering_action: Add to low-urgency outputs a standing prompt to seek care if symptoms persist or worsen, plus uncertainty cues. Document the automation-bias measures in the oversight instructions for deployers and caregivers.

addressed_by.covers: ability to challenge or dismiss AI suggestions (14(4)(d))
clinical review of high-risk outputs (14(4)(c)-(d))

recommendations: Rewrite NFR-15.5 with a measurable under-triage threshold, a pre-release test protocol and vulnerable-group (older adult) test coverage, and record false reassurance in the risk management file.
Define and monitor accuracy metrics for urgency classification and declare the achieved levels in the instructions for use.
Add automation-bias safeguards for reassuring outputs, such as standing 'seek care if symptoms persist' prompts, and document them in the oversight instructions.

requirement_text: The app shall comply with recognised accessibility guidelines such as WCAG 2.2 where applicable.

assessment.summary: NFR-2.1 is itself an accessibility control, but it names only WCAG 2.2 "where applicable" and does not tie it to the legal accessibility requirements in Article 16(1)(l). It also does not say that AI-interaction and AI-generated-content disclosures must meet those requirements. These are wording and evidence gaps, not missing controls.

risks.description: The requirement uses a soft "such as WCAG 2.2 where applicable" standard and does not name Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882, so it gives no testable basis for showing the legally required accessibility conformance if the system is high-risk (e.g. medical-device or triage functions).
risks.quote: ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.
risks.engineering_action: Reword to require conformance with the accessibility requirements of Directives 2016/2102 and 2019/882 (WCAG 2.2 AA as the technical baseline). Define which screens are in scope, and record accessibility test evidence in the technical documentation and conformity file.

addressed_by.covers: screen-reader support as an accessibility feature
high-contrast display option
voice input and audio output
support for reduced vision, hearing, dexterity or cognitive ability

risks.description: The requirement does not state that the notices telling users they are interacting with an AI system or viewing AI-generated content (FR-3.1, FR-11.5) must themselves meet the applicable accessibility requirements, such as screen-reader and voice delivery.
risks.quote: The information shall conform to the applicable accessibility requirements.
risks.engineering_action: Add an acceptance criterion that AI-interaction and AI-generated-content disclosures are accessible (screen-reader compatible, voice-readable, high contrast, shown at first interaction) and cover them in accessibility testing.

addressed_by.covers: screen-reader support, which can carry AI disclosures
audio output, which can carry AI disclosures

recommendations: Tie NFR-2.1 to Directives 2016/2102 and 2019/882, with WCAG 2.2 AA as a mandatory baseline, a defined scope, and retained test evidence.
Explicitly include AI disclosure and transparency notices in the accessibility acceptance criteria.

requirement_text: The app shall allow users to slow down or repeat voice instructions.

assessment.summary: NFR-2.8 is an accessibility convenience feature (slow down or repeat voice instructions). It does not touch any high-risk function and no cited AI Act provision imposes a requirement-level obligation on it.

requirement_text: The app shall escalate potentially serious symptoms to emergency or professional care guidance.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.2 sets the escalation behaviour but gives no definition of 'potentially serious', no sensitivity or false-negative targets, and no fail-safe if detection fails. A missed escalation for an older adult is a direct health-safety risk. The system looks like emergency healthcare triage (Annex III 5(d)) or medical-device functionality, so confirm classification; the risks below assume it is high-risk.

risks.description: The escalation trigger ('potentially serious symptoms') has no defined criteria, no target sensitivity or false-negative rate, and no acceptance threshold, so missed escalations are not controlled or declared.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Define clinically validated escalation criteria and metrics (e.g. minimum sensitivity for urgent/emergency cases, maximum false-negative rate). Test against them before release and after model or knowledge-base updates. Declare the resulting levels in the instructions for use (Art. 15(3)).

addressed_by.covers: classification of symptoms by urgency level
detection of emergency keywords or severe symptoms with urgent-action recommendation

risks.description: No fail-safe behaviour is specified for escalation when the AI classification is uncertain, errors out, or the network or service is down, so a serious symptom could be silently under-escalated.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be as resilient as possible regarding errors, faults or inconsistencies that may occur within the system or the environment in which the system operates
risks.engineering_action: Add a fail-safe rule: when severity is uncertain or classification fails, default to showing emergency/professional-care guidance. Make the escalation path work offline using local rules. Test it under fault injection.

addressed_by.covers: emergency information remains accessible during service disruption
offline access to emergency contacts

risks.description: The requirement does not state that escalation events (trigger inputs, severity assigned, guidance shown, user response) are recorded, which limits traceability and post-market review of missed or wrong escalations.
risks.quote: logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for: (a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk
risks.engineering_action: Specify that each escalation decision is logged with inputs, urgency level, guidance shown, model version and user action. Retain the logs for at least six months.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for audit and safety review

recommendations: Define clinically validated escalation criteria with sensitivity and false-negative targets, test against them, and declare the achieved levels in the instructions for use.
Add a default-to-escalate fail-safe for uncertain or failed classification, including an offline path.
Explicitly log every escalation decision and the user's response to it.

requirement_text: The app shall include safeguards against hallucinated medical advice.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.4 states the intent to guard against hallucinated medical advice but names no safeguard, metric, or acceptance threshold. If the app is high-risk (emergency triage in Annex III 5(d), or medical device functionality), the safeguard cannot be tested or shown to meet accuracy, robustness and risk-management obligations.

risks.description: The safeguard has no defined mechanism, hallucination or accuracy metric, or pass/fail threshold, so it cannot be verified before release or monitored over the lifecycle.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and that they perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle.
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite the requirement to name concrete safeguards (e.g. grounding in vetted sources, output validation, refusal on low confidence). Define measurable hallucination and factual-accuracy metrics with acceptance thresholds and a regression test suite, including after model updates.

risks.description: No requirement says that testing against prior-defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds is done for medical-advice hallucination before release.
risks.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Add a pre-release test requirement: a clinician-curated adversarial and edge-case question set for older-adult scenarios, with documented thresholds, results and sign-off. Re-run it on every model or knowledge-base change.

risks.description: Resilience of the hallucination safeguards against adversarial or manipulated inputs (prompt injection, jailbreaks, confusing voice or text input) is not specified.
risks.quote: The technical solutions to address AI specific vulnerabilities shall include, where appropriate, measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for attacks trying to manipulate the training data set (data poisoning), or pre-trained components used in training (model poisoning), inputs designed to cause the AI model to make a mistake (adversarial examples or model evasion), confidentiality attacks or model flaws.
risks.engineering_action: Require adversarial and prompt-injection testing of the AI assistant with input and output guardrails that keep the medical-safety safeguards active. Cover these cases in security testing.

risks.description: The accuracy level and metrics that users and deployers can expect, including known hallucination limits, are not declared in any instructions for use.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Add an SRS requirement for instructions for use that declare measured accuracy and hallucination metrics and known limitations. Keep them in step with test results.

recommendations: Make NFR-3.4 specific: name the safeguard mechanisms and define measurable hallucination and accuracy metrics with thresholds.
Add pre-release and post-update testing against pre-defined metrics, using a clinician-curated adversarial test set.
Add adversarial and prompt-injection resilience requirements for the AI assistant.
Add a requirement to declare accuracy levels, metrics and limitations in instructions for use.

requirement_text: The app shall provide clear emergency instructions when urgent symptoms are detected.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.5 is a safety control that only fixes the output (clear emergency instructions). It says nothing about how reliably urgent symptoms are detected, how that is tested, or whether instructions still appear when the AI path fails. Triage with missed urgent cases could harm older adults, and the SRS declares no accuracy metrics for detection. This assumes the app is high-risk (medical-device or emergency-triage context), which the SRS does not state outright.

risks.description: No accuracy level or metric (including false-negative rate for urgent/emergency symptoms) is defined for the detection that triggers these instructions, so none can be declared in the instructions for use.
risks.quote: The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics of high-risk AI systems shall be declared in the accompanying instructions of use.
risks.engineering_action: Define sensitivity/specificity targets for urgent and emergency classes, with a minimum false-negative threshold. Validate them on representative older-adult data and declare them in the instructions for use.

risks.description: The requirement has no pre-defined test metrics, thresholds or acceptance criteria for verifying that emergency instructions are triggered correctly. The SRS has no risk management process covering missed or delayed urgent detection.
risks.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Add a documented risk management process with hazard analysis for missed or delayed urgent detection. Add test cases and acceptance thresholds for the emergency-instruction path, run before release and after each model update.

addressed_by.covers: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs (a risk control measure under 9(2)(d))

risks.description: The wording does not require the emergency instructions to be delivered on a deterministic, fail-safe path that works if the AI service, network or detection component errors or is unavailable.
risks.quote: The robustness of high-risk AI systems may be achieved through technical redundancy solutions, which may include backup or fail-safe plans.
risks.engineering_action: Reword NFR-3.5 so that emergency instructions are served from static, locally cached content. Add a rule-based fallback trigger if the AI classifier fails or times out.

addressed_by.covers: emergency information remains accessible during service disruption (fail-safe availability)
offline access to emergency contacts

recommendations: Define and validate accuracy metrics (especially false-negative rate) for urgent and emergency symptom detection, and declare them in the instructions for use.
Establish a risk management process with pre-defined test metrics and thresholds for the emergency-instruction path, re-run on every model update.
Reword NFR-3.5 to require fail-safe, locally cached, rule-based emergency instructions that work when the AI service or network is unavailable.

requirement_text: The app shall log AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review.

assessment.summary: NFR-3.6 logs only the AI-generated advice text. It does not specify the events, context or retention that Article 12 and 19 logging needs for risk identification, post-market monitoring and deployer oversight. Auditors could not reconstruct why unsafe advice was given or spot emerging risks. The analysis assumes the app may be high-risk, for example through emergency or patient triage in Annex III point 5(d) or medical-device scope.

risks.description: Logging is limited to the advice output. It does not capture inputs, model/knowledge-base version, urgency classification, confidence, user dismissals or challenges, or escalation events. It also does not say logging is automatic over the system lifetime, so risk situations and substantial modifications cannot be traced.
risks.quote: logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for: (a) identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) or in a substantial modification;
risks.engineering_action: Rewrite as: the system shall automatically log, for each AI interaction, the input context, model and knowledge-base version, output, urgency class, confidence, user actions (dismiss, challenge, report) and escalations. Make the log tamper-evident and active for the system lifetime.

risks.description: No log retention period is stated, and no minimum of six months is set. 'Auditing and safety review' gives no retention, access or deletion rules for AI logs, which also hold health data.
risks.quote: the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
risks.engineering_action: Specify an AI-log retention period of at least six months (longer if justified by clinical safety needs). Define access controls and a pseudonymisation or deletion schedule consistent with data protection law.

risks.description: The requirement does not say how logs support post-market monitoring or deployer monitoring. There is no mechanism for deployers (clinicians, operators) to collect, store and interpret the logs, and no link to incident analysis.
risks.quote: a description of the mechanisms included within the high-risk AI system that allows deployers to properly collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12.
risks.engineering_action: Add log export and query capability for authorised deployers and the provider, and document the log format and interpretation in the instructions for use. Feed the logs into the post-market monitoring process.

recommendations: Expand NFR-3.6 into an automatic, tamper-evident event log covering inputs, model version, output, urgency classification, user overrides and escalations over the system lifetime.
Define an AI log retention period of at least six months, with access control and a deletion schedule.
Provide deployer and provider log access and export, and document log interpretation in the instructions for use.

requirement_text: The app shall obtain user consent before collecting, storing, or sharing health information.

assessment.summary: NFR-4.2 is a GDPR-style consent control and mostly sits outside the AI Act, which defers to data protection law (Art 2(7)). The only remaining gap is that consent for collecting, storing and sharing does not address the AI Act's strict conditions for processing health data (special categories) for bias detection and correction.

risks.description: Consent covers collection, storage and sharing, but not secondary use of health data (special categories) for bias examination or correction of the AI. Art 10(5) requires specific safeguards for that use: necessity, no re-use or transfer, access controls, deletion and documentation.
risks.quote: the providers of such systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data, subject to appropriate safeguards for the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons
risks.engineering_action: Extend the consent scope to cover use of health data for bias detection and model evaluation. Document the Art 10(5)(a)-(f) controls for that processing: strict necessity, pseudonymisation, restricted access, no third-party transfer, deletion after bias correction, and records of processing.

addressed_by.covers: anonymisation or de-identification of data used for model improvement (partial support for 10(5)(a)-(b))
process for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (10(2)(f))

recommendations: Add a consent and safeguard clause for secondary use of health data in bias detection and model evaluation, aligned with Art 10(5) conditions and documented in the data governance records.

requirement_text: The app shall allow users to view, edit, export, or delete their personal data.

assessment.summary: NFR-4.3 gives users view/edit/export/delete rights over their personal data. This is a GDPR-style data-subject control, not an AI Act obligation. The only AI Act link is that edit/delete could alter data used for training or logs, which this requirement does not address.

risks.description: User edit/delete of personal data could change or remove data held in records the Act requires (e.g. AI-advice logs, clinical audit records, training/validation/testing data), and the requirement does not say how this is reconciled with log retention and data governance.
risks.quote: the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data.
risks.engineering_action: State that deletion/edit requests are applied to user-facing data, while required audit logs (NFR-3.6, NFR-13.3) are retained for the legally required period, pseudonymised where possible. Document how edits to inputs are versioned so past AI outputs remain traceable.

addressed_by.covers: logging of AI-generated advice for auditing, in line with Art. 12 automatic event recording
data retention and deletion policies, which can set the retention period for logs

recommendations: Add a retention/deletion exception clause so that user deletion does not remove legally required audit logs, and document how edited data is versioned for traceability.

requirement_text: The app shall anonymise or de-identify data where used for analytics or model improvement.

assessment.summary: NFR-4.6 is a privacy-protective control (anonymise or de-identify analytics and model-improvement data), but it sets no standard or verification for anonymisation quality. It also does not address the bias-examination and data-governance practices that apply when that data is reused to improve a health-related model.

risks.description: Reuse of data for model improvement is not tied to documented data governance (origin, original collection purpose, preparation steps, suitability), and de-identification may remove attributes needed to examine bias across age, gender or health condition.
risks.quote: data collection processes and the origin of data, and in the case of personal data, the original purpose of the data collection;
risks.engineering_action: Add data governance procedures for model-improvement datasets. Record provenance and original collection purpose, define the anonymisation method and re-identification risk testing, and retain the attributes (or privacy-preserving proxies) needed for bias examination.

addressed_by.covers: processes for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (partial coverage of examining possible biases, 10(2)(f))
data minimisation: collect only health data necessary for intended functions

risks.description: Training, validation and testing data produced by de-identification have no stated quality criteria (representativeness, error-freeness, statistical properties for older-adult subgroups), so anonymisation could degrade dataset suitability unnoticed.
risks.quote: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose.
risks.engineering_action: Define and test acceptance criteria for de-identified datasets (completeness, representativeness across age, gender, conditions and languages) before use in model improvement, and document the results.

recommendations: Add provenance, purpose and preparation documentation, with bias-aware anonymisation, for any data reused in model improvement.
Define and verify quality acceptance criteria for de-identified training, validation and testing datasets.

requirement_text: The app shall support secure authentication, such as passwords, PINs, biometrics, or multi-factor authentication.

assessment.summary: NFR-5.2 is a general authentication requirement that supports secure access. The system's Annex III classification is not stated, and no cybersecurity provision cited here is specific to authentication, so the only gap is that Article 15 cybersecurity wording is not tied to the AI-specific attack surface.

risks.description: The requirement lists generic user authentication options but does not address resilience against unauthorised third parties altering the AI system's use, outputs or performance (e.g. admin/model-update access, manipulation of inputs), nor require authentication strength appropriate to the risk of health data and AI model access.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Clarify that MFA is mandatory for caregiver, clinician and administrator roles and for any access to AI model configuration/updates. Document in the technical documentation how authentication fits the AI-specific threat model, alongside the existing security testing and access control requirements.

addressed_by.covers: role-based access control limiting who can use or change the system
security testing and vulnerability assessments to detect exploitable weaknesses
protection against unauthorised access to health records

recommendations: Make MFA mandatory for privileged roles (clinician, caregiver, administrator) and for AI model/configuration access, and record the authentication design in the Article 15 cybersecurity documentation.

requirement_text: The app shall maintain audit logs for access to sensitive information.

assessment.summary: NFR-5.5 covers only access logging for sensitive data, which is a security and privacy control. It does not state log content, retention or integrity, so it does not satisfy the Act's automatic event recording for a potentially high-risk health-triage system (FR-4.3 classifies symptoms up to 'emergency'). Other requirements log AI advice and caregiver actions, so what remains is traceability of the AI system's own events plus retention and integrity of the logs.

risks.description: Audit logging is scoped to access to sensitive information, so events relevant to identifying AI risk, post-market monitoring and operational monitoring (model version, inputs, urgency classification, user overrides or challenges, model updates) are not required to be recorded; NFR-3.6 covers only AI-generated advice.
risks.quote: logging capabilities shall enable the recording of events relevant for:
risks.engineering_action: Define a logging specification covering AI-system events: inputs, outputs, urgency classification, model and knowledge-base version, user challenge or dismiss actions, and model updates. Link it to post-market monitoring, and state that NFR-5.5 access logs are one stream within it.

addressed_by.covers: automatic recording of AI-generated advice for auditing and safety review (part of the 12(1) and 12(2) event recording)
activity log of caregiver actions

risks.description: NFR-5.5 sets no retention period, tamper protection or access restriction for the audit logs, so the minimum six-month retention for automatically generated logs is not assured and log integrity is not specified.
risks.quote: the logs shall be kept for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months
risks.engineering_action: Amend NFR-5.5 to specify a log retention period of at least six months, aligned with data protection law. Add append-only or tamper-evident storage and restrict log access to authorised roles.

recommendations: Define a system-wide AI event logging specification (inputs, outputs, classifications, model versions, overrides) and relate NFR-5.5 and NFR-3.6 to it.
Add retention (at least six months), integrity protection and access control for audit logs to NFR-5.5.

requirement_text: The app shall use role-based access control for older adults, caregivers, clinicians, and administrators.

assessment.summary: The RBAC requirement lists roles but does not say what each role may do with the AI components (models, configuration, logs, training data), so the administrator role could alter AI outputs without control. It also does not tie the clinician role to review or override of AI outputs. This assessment assumes the app is high-risk (e.g. symptom urgency triage in FR-4.3, or medical device functionality); that classification needs confirming.

risks.description: RBAC is defined only at role level and does not cover privileges over AI components (model updates, thresholds, knowledge base, logs, training data). A compromised or over-privileged administrator account could alter AI outputs or performance.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be resilient against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter their use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities.
risks.engineering_action: Define a permission matrix covering AI assets (model deployment, configuration, knowledge base, log access, training data). Apply least privilege, require MFA and separation of duties for administrator and model-change actions, and log those actions.

addressed_by.covers: audit logs for access to sensitive information, supporting detection of unauthorised access

risks.description: The clinician role is not linked to oversight capabilities. The requirement does not give clinicians or caregivers defined permissions to review, override, or stop AI outputs and recommendations.
risks.quote: to decide, in any particular situation, not to use the high-risk AI system or to otherwise disregard, override or reverse the output of the high-risk AI system;
risks.engineering_action: Specify that the clinician role holds permissions to review flagged AI outputs, override or reverse recommendations, and suspend AI features per user. Enforce these through RBAC.

addressed_by.covers: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs
users can challenge, correct or dismiss AI suggestions

recommendations: Extend NFR-5.6 with a permission matrix that covers AI assets, least privilege, MFA and separation of duties for administrators, and logging of privileged actions.
Define clinician (and, where relevant, caregiver) permissions to review, override and halt AI outputs, and enforce them through RBAC.

requirement_text: The app shall prevent data loss during crashes or connectivity interruptions.

assessment.summary: NFR-6.4 is a general data-preservation requirement with no specific EU AI Act obligation. Its robustness aspect (Art. 15(4)) is largely covered by other SRS requirements, so no requirement-level gap remains.

requirement_text: The app shall respond quickly to user interactions.

assessment.summary: NFR-7.2 is a generic responsiveness requirement with no direct EU AI Act obligation. Performance targets for the AI assistant are covered by NFR-7.3, and accuracy, robustness and safety are addressed elsewhere in the SRS.

requirement_text: The AI assistant shall provide responses within an acceptable timeframe.

assessment.summary: NFR-7.3 sets no measurable latency target for the AI assistant, so response-time performance cannot be tested against pre-defined metrics. This matters if the assistant's symptom-urgency and emergency guidance puts the system in a high-risk class. The gap is a wording clarification and does not by itself breach an obligation.

risks.description: "Acceptable timeframe" is undefined and untestable, with no latency thresholds, percentiles, or stricter targets for urgent-symptom and emergency responses, so testing against pre-defined metrics is not possible.
risks.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Replace "acceptable" with quantified targets (e.g. p95 latency under X s for general queries, a stricter bound for urgent and emergency flows). Define degraded-mode behaviour, such as static emergency guidance, when the target is missed. Add these targets to the test plan and the declared performance metrics.

recommendations: Quantify the response-time criteria in NFR-7.3, with separate stricter thresholds and a fallback for urgent and emergency interactions, and make them part of the pre-release test plan.

requirement_text: The app shall support offline access to essential information such as medication schedules and emergency contacts.

assessment.summary: Offline access to medication schedules and emergency contacts is a availability/usability feature. The provisions show no requirement-level gap, but offline cached data may need consistency and integrity controls that are better handled elsewhere in the SRS.

requirement_text: The app shall regularly update its medical knowledge base.

assessment.summary: The requirement says only that the medical knowledge base is updated "regularly". It sets no cadence, source provenance, pre-release testing or change-control criteria. If the app is high-risk (e.g. emergency triage under Annex III 5(d), or a medical device), unvalidated updates could change health outputs after conformity assessment without being assessed.

risks.description: Knowledge-base updates have no requirement for testing against predefined accuracy metrics and thresholds before release, so recommendation quality could regress silently.
risks.quote: Testing shall be carried out against prior defined metrics and probabilistic thresholds that are appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system.
risks.engineering_action: Require each knowledge-base update to pass regression and clinical-safety tests against predefined metrics and thresholds, with rollback on failure, before release.

addressed_by.covers: correction or removal of inaccurate recommendations after they are identified (reactive only, not pre-release testing)

risks.description: The requirement does not say how an update is assessed as a substantial modification or as a pre-determined change, so updates could alter the assessed system without re-assessment or documentation.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems that have already been subject to a conformity assessment procedure shall undergo a new conformity assessment procedure in the event of a substantial modification
risks.engineering_action: Add a change-control step that classifies each update as pre-determined or substantial, records it in the technical documentation, and triggers re-assessment where needed.

risks.description: "Regularly" is undefined, and the requirement does not name the origin or provenance of update content or how it is selected and prepared, so data governance of the knowledge base cannot be shown.
risks.quote: data collection processes and the origin of data
risks.engineering_action: Define the update cadence and triggers, approved sources, and a provenance and versioning record for each update.

addressed_by.covers: recommendations based on reliable medical knowledge sources (source reliability only; no provenance or versioning records)

recommendations: Gate every knowledge-base update on pre-release testing against predefined metrics and thresholds, with rollback.
Add change control that classifies updates as pre-determined or substantial and feeds the technical documentation and any re-assessment.
Specify the update cadence, approved sources and a provenance and version log for knowledge-base content.

requirement_text: The system shall support regular software updates and bug fixes.

assessment.summary: The requirement only says updates and bug fixes are supported. It has no change-control rule for classifying an update as a substantial modification, re-testing performance, or keeping the technical documentation current. If the system is high-risk (for example, medical-device AI), updates could invalidate conformity or degrade performance without detection.

risks.description: No rule for assessing whether an update or AI model change is a 'substantial modification' that triggers a new conformity assessment, or for separating pre-determined changes from unplanned ones.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems that have already been subject to a conformity assessment procedure shall undergo a new conformity assessment procedure in the event of a substantial modification
risks.engineering_action: Add a release-gating step that classifies each update (including AI model and knowledge-base updates) against substantial-modification criteria. Record pre-determined changes in the technical documentation, and trigger re-assessment when a change falls outside them.

risks.description: Updates are not tied to regression testing against predefined accuracy and robustness metrics, so performance may drift after a release.
risks.quote: perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle
risks.engineering_action: Require that every update passes regression tests against declared accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity thresholds before release, with rollback if they fail.

addressed_by.covers: testing of individual modules (reminders, AI assistant, notifications, data sharing), a partial basis for pre-release testing

risks.description: No obligation to keep technical documentation, the risk management file and the QMS change-management procedures up to date with each update.
risks.quote: shall be drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up-to date
risks.engineering_action: Make a documentation update (Annex IV, including the description of relevant changes through the lifecycle) part of the release definition of done. Link it to a QMS procedure for managing modifications.

addressed_by.covers: maintaining documentation for developers and administrators, but not Annex IV compliance documentation

recommendations: Add a change-classification gate to the update process to decide whether a release is a substantial modification and needs re-assessment.
Require regression testing against predefined accuracy and robustness metrics, with rollback, for every update.
Include the Annex IV technical documentation and QMS change records in the release checklist.

requirement_text: The system shall allow older adults to create an account using email, phone number, or caregiver-assisted registration.

assessment.summary: FR-1.1 is an account-creation function and does not itself perform AI processing. None of the supplied provisions (registration, authorised representatives, transparency to deployers, etc.) imposes an obligation at the level of this requirement.

requirement_text: The system shall support different user roles, including older adult, caregiver, doctor, nurse, and administrator.

assessment.summary: FR-1.5 only lists user roles and says nothing about how role-specific oversight or competence is supported. The provisions give only a thin basis for a requirement-level gap: role definitions do not make clinician and caregiver oversight effective, and no role-specific literacy or training support is stated.

risks.description: Roles such as doctor, nurse and caregiver are listed, but the requirement does not define role-specific interfaces or capabilities (review, override, escalation) that would let those roles oversee the AI outputs effectively.
risks.quote: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.
risks.engineering_action: Specify per role (doctor, nurse, caregiver) the oversight functions available, such as reviewing, overriding and escalating AI outputs, and link them to NFR-8.6 and NFR-15.4.

addressed_by.covers: clinical review of high-risk AI outputs by a human
user ability to challenge, correct or dismiss AI suggestions

risks.description: The requirement does not tie roles to AI-literacy support, so older adults, caregivers and clinicians using the AI outputs may lack role-appropriate guidance on their use and limits.
risks.quote: taking into account their technical knowledge, experience, education and training and the context the AI systems are to be used in
risks.engineering_action: Add role-tailored onboarding and AI-limitation guidance for each role, building on NFR-1.6 and NFR-1.7.

addressed_by.covers: guided onboarding for first-time users

recommendations: Define role-specific oversight capabilities (review, override, escalation) for clinician and caregiver roles.
Add role-tailored onboarding and AI-literacy content for each user role.

requirement_text: The system shall provide access to mental health helplines or support resources.

assessment.summary: FR-10.4 (providing mental health helplines or support resources) is a supportive safeguard, and none of the supplied provisions impose an obligation on this requirement. The provisions concern authorities, experts, representatives and other matters unrelated to it.

requirement_text: The system shall generate personalised health reminders based on the user’s age, health conditions, medication schedule, and activity patterns.

assessment.summary: FR-11.1 personalises reminders from age, health conditions, medication and activity data, but states no bias, representativeness or foreseeable-risk controls for vulnerable older users. If the system is high-risk, wrong or age-biased reminders (for example a missed or mistimed medication cue) could harm health, and the SRS has no risk management process to catch this.

risks.description: No risk identification or mitigation is defined for reminders that depend on health and medication data for an older, vulnerable user group; wrong, mistimed or missing reminders could cause health harm.
risks.quote: the identification and analysis of the known and the reasonably foreseeable risks that the high-risk AI system can pose to health, safety or fundamental rights when the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with its intended purpose
risks.engineering_action: Establish a lifecycle risk management process covering reminder-generation hazards (wrong timing or content, missed critical reminders, conflicts with medication data). Define risk acceptance criteria and mitigations such as clinical-rule guardrails and fallback to the user's fixed medication schedule.

risks.description: The requirement does not state that age-based personalisation will specifically consider adverse impact on older or otherwise vulnerable users, such as cognitive impairment or frailty.
risks.quote: providers shall give consideration to whether in view of its intended purpose the high-risk AI system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under the age of 18 and, as appropriate, other vulnerable groups
risks.engineering_action: Document a vulnerable-group impact assessment for personalised reminders. Add constraints that age is used only for clinically justified adaptation, and validate with cognitively impaired users.

addressed_by.covers: avoiding ageist assumptions in design and recommendations

risks.description: Bias review is required by NFR-12.7, but there is no requirement for mitigation measures or for representative datasets across age, condition and activity profiles used to personalise reminders.
risks.quote: appropriate measures to detect, prevent and mitigate possible biases identified according to point (f)
risks.engineering_action: Add acceptance criteria and mitigation steps for bias found in reminder personalisation. Require data-representativeness checks (10(3)) across age bands, conditions and activity levels, and record data gaps.

addressed_by.covers: process for reviewing bias in AI recommendations (10(2)(f))

recommendations: Create a lifecycle risk management process for personalised reminder hazards, with acceptance criteria and mitigations such as clinical-rule guardrails and fallback to the fixed medication schedule.
Document a vulnerable-group (older adult) impact assessment and limit age use to clinically justified adaptation.
Define bias mitigation measures and data representativeness checks for the personalisation inputs (age, conditions, medication, activity).

requirement_text: The system shall allow users to customise notification frequency and style.

assessment.summary: FR-12.2 lets users customise notification frequency and style. None of the supplied provisions (Articles 27, 28-31, 36, 37, 45, 112 and the Article 3 definitions) concern the obligations of AI system providers or deployers for user-facing notification settings. They govern notifying authorities and notified bodies, so no requirement-level compliance gap arises.

requirement_text: The system shall avoid excessive notifications to reduce confusion or alarm.

assessment.summary: FR-12.5 is a UX requirement about limiting notification volume. The supplied provisions (Articles 28-52, 79, 80, 90) concern notified bodies, notifying authorities and authority procedures, not in-app user notifications, so no requirement-level compliance gap is supported.

requirement_text: The system shall highlight important changes, missed medications, abnormal readings, or recurring symptoms.

assessment.summary: FR-13.5 highlights changes, missed medications, abnormal readings and recurring symptoms in health summaries, but the supplied provisions (mostly notified-body, GPAI and Commission procedures) support only a post-market monitoring gap, and the Act's classification of this system as high-risk is not established here. The requirement defines no detection criteria and no feedback loop to collect experience on whether highlights are missed or wrong.

risks.description: No documented post-market monitoring system or plan collects and reviews field experience on whether the highlighting (abnormal readings, recurring symptoms) misses or wrongly flags events, so corrective action cannot be triggered.
